(nee Somerville) and her brother Reginald M J B Somerville and registered in the Irish Genealogical Office. A copy of this Pedigree was given to DRG Gilmour by Dorothy Rooke, daughter of Cecilia E M B Rooke and is referred to elsewhere in the profiles of James Somerville and his descendants as the ‘Somerville Index’.

While the entries in the Somerville Index are largely correct, a more detailed pedigree was drawn up at a later date by the Lancaster Herald in The College of Arms, Queen Victoria St., London from further information supplied by Reginald M J B Somerville and his youngest sister Edeline B M B Hill with a view to recording it officially with the College; the descendants of Archibald James Somerville and Corry Somerville, the 2nd and 3rd sons of Capt William Somerville and his wife, Eliza, nee Bellingham , respectively were not included as, at the time, there was no certainty that their children were legitimate. Since that time, it has been conclusively established that the children of Corry and his wife, Lucinda, nee Simonton, were legitimate and they are therefore included among the profiles. This pedigree went before the Chapter of the College as part of the procedure for recording, but Garter King of Arms, who happened to be present, wanted to consider the matter further, in particular, the background to the entries for Archibald James and Corry. Nothing further was heard from Garter or the College and the pedigree , therefore, remains in draft form only.

It is believed that James Somerville, The Planter, was the natural son, and, therefore, without right of primogeniture, of James Somerville 4th Baron of Cambusnethan [Memorie of the Somervilles Vol 1;p387] known as ‘Velvet Eye’.[Vol 2;Pg89]. James (Velvet Eye) was the eldest son of John Somerville, 3rd Baron of Cambusnethan known as ‘The Laird with the Plaides’ [Vol1;p415&497] by his 1st wife, Katherine Carmichael [Vol1;p385/7]; subsequently, after Katherine Carmichael’s death, John, 3rd Baron, married Katherine Murray, daughter of Patrick Murray of Philliphaughes [Vol 1;p427] in 1552 and had a further eight children. Velvet Eye married Margaret Hamilton, daughter of Archibald Hamilton of Raploch [Vol 1;p428&Vol 2;p88], and they had three children, John, Margaret and Mary. He also had a natural son, James, of whom the writer of the Memorie says he’ cannot give any account’, [Vol2;p89]. However, the writer of this profile has seen a statement, he cannot now recall where, that the natural son ‘disappeared into Ireland’. Velvet Eye died in 1623.

There is another theory that James the Planter was descended from Hugh Somerville, 5th Lord Somerville,11th Baron of Linton, 8th Baron of Carnwarth (1485-1550). Hugh married 1st 1510 Anne, daughter of James Hamilton,1st Earl of Arran; she died 1516 without issue. He married 2nd 1517 Janet, daughter of William Maitland of Leidington (Secretary to Queen Mary). Hugh had 4 sons and 3 daughters by his 2nd marriage and died in 1550.His eldest son James became 6th Lord Somerville, 12th Baron of Linton and 9th Baron of Carnwarth (1519-1570). James (6th Lord) married 1540 Agnes, daughter of Sir James Hamilton of Finnart. James (6th Lord) and his wife Agnes had 2 sons and 2 daughters, namely, Hugh who became 7th Lord, James who, according to the Memorie, received part of the lands of Carnwarth and married a daughter of Laird Lindsay of Covington, Margaret and Agnes. This theory suggests that James, the younger son of James, 6th Lord Somerville, who was alledgedly born in 1555 married Elizabeth, daughter of Thomas Hamilton of Brimhill and was the Planter. This contradicts the account in the Memorie unless the daughter of Laird Lindsay of Covington died and James married Elizabeth Hamilton, daughter of Thomas Hamilton of Brimhill as his 2nd Wife.. The Memorie is silent as to the life of James, the younger son of 6th Lord Somerville, apart from his marriage to the daughter of Laird Lindsay of Covington.

In Ireland following the Nine Years War (1594-1603), a negotiated settlement allowed the reinstatement of most of their ancestral lands to the Irish. The Irish had held out for a long time in Ulster; most of the other three provinces had been subjected to some element of English rule by the end of the main conflict following the Battle of Kinsale. After 4 years of further unrest in Ulster’, the northern Gaelic chiefs took ship at Rathmullen in 1607 for the continent, going into voluntary exile in Spain. The ‘Flight of the Earls’ as it became known left Ulster leaderless, lands had been forfeited and the way was open for a new plantation.

There was a continual fear that Ireland would be used as a base for foreign enemies to attack the mainland of England and Scotland. There had been previous attempts to settle, or plant, English settlors in Leinster and Munster, with a view to civilizing the Irish and providing protection for England; these were relatively small settlements, apart from the Norman conquest, and were relatively unplanned and unsuccessful. In Ulster arrangements were detailed in advance and guarantees were required to meet certain plantation expectations, failing which land would be forfeited and revert to the Crown. Land was granted to English and Scottish settlors or ‘Planters’ on condition that they built strongholds and occupied the land; in particular not allowing it to be occupied by ‘meer Irish’. To effect the Plantation, settlors, named ‘undertakers’, who were civilians, had to settle ten English or Scottish families on each 1,000 acres of , ‘improved’ or profitable land received in the grant. There was also another class of settlor named ‘servitors’ who were generally former soldiers who were granted leases by the undertakers in exchange for occupation of part of the undertakers’ grant. The grant to the undertakers also included large areas of unimproved land substantially in excess of the areas mentioned in the records.

At the time of the Plantation, 4 separate Hamilton families received lands from James 1 in Cos Tyrone, Armagh, Cavan and Fermanagh. According to Lord Belmore’s history of the Hamilton family in Co Fermanagh, Robert Hamilton, 2nd son of James Hamilton of Stanehouse in Lanarkshire applied for 1,500 acres, part of an estate of more than 10,000 acres in the Barony of Magheraboy in Co Fermanagh in 1609, receiving the grant in 1610. He took possession of his land at Derrinfogher in Devenish Parish in Co Fermanagh (4 miles west of Enniskillen ) with a party of 18. Four years later, he sold 1,000 acres to his brother Malcolm Hamilton and 500 acres to his brother Archibald Hamilton.

Lord Belmore describes the plantation of Derrinfogher and cites the account of Pynnar in his Survey of Ulster, 1618-1619: ‘I find planted and estated upon this land of British Birth and Descent 3 Freeholders,1 having 384 acres, 1 having 120 acres and 1 having 60 acres…11 Lessees, 3 having 180 acres jointly, 3 having 120 acres le piece, 2 having 40 acres le piece and 1 having 20 acres’. Pynnar further says ‘Of all these tenants, there are seven of them have taken the Oath of Supremacy and these have divers under- tenants under them, all of which are able to make seventy seven men with reasonable Arms. There is good store of Tillage, and not an Irish family on all the Lands.’ Trimble in History of Enniskillen says that Captain Pynnar names the Freeholders as Robert Weir, Gabriel Cunningham and James Somerville holding (unidentified) 384 ac, 120ac and 60ac.

Lord Belmore states that the Inquisition held at Myneagh(Monea) provided that ‘the late King James, on the 20th August of the 8th year of his reign of England and 44th of Scotland (1610) was seized in fee in right of his Crown of Ireland of the middle portion of Derrinfogher etc. (and it sets out 36 denominations of land besides the islands of Fusie and Cloynecushine, estimated at 1,500 acres more or less), with free fishing in Lough Erne .. .and granted this portion to Robert Hamilton on condition that if he alienated the premises to any persons being ‘meer’ Irish or to any person who, within twelve months of such alienation, had not taken the Oath of Supremacy, then the said Letters Patent should be void. On 20th August 1621, the Inquisition goes on to show that Malcolm Hamilton who had bought the land from his brother Robert enfeoffed Robert Weir of Tullymargy,gent, Gabriel Coningham,gent and James Somerville of the whole portion, ‘except p except’ in trust for such uses as he should declare in writing in his will’.
Inquisitions were enquiries as to progress being made in the Plantation and were held regularly, reporting to the King.

All this puts James Somerville, the Planter, in possession of land at Derrinfogher in the parish of Devenish, in Co Fermanagh in 1610 as tenant in freehold of Malcolm Hamilton of Monea, who became Archbishop of Cashel in 1623.

On 13th March, 1615 Malcolm Hamilton granted to James Somerville and Elizabeth his wife the parcels of land called Tullacalter, Tullykelter, Tullenmlinora, Dromscobbe and Carrinmore. Elizabeth Somerville was a Hamilton from Brimhill in Lanarkshire; specifically, a document at PRONI T2615/10, quoted by The Rev J H Steele , states that ’James Somerville of Tullykelter Castle (of the House of Cambusnethan,Agr.,)obtained a grant from Malcolm Hamilton 13 March 1615 of the lands of Tullykelter, Drumscollop and Carran’. The writer suspects the foregoing quotation is from Mr Steele’s paper rather than the grant itself, but it is important, nonetheless, as it links James Somerville with the House of Cambusnethan for the first time in the surviving Somerville Records; he also suspects that the word or abbreviation ‘Agr’ is not a misprint for the County of AYR , as has frequently been suggested, but is the abbreviation for ‘Agricola’ or ‘Farmer’. All the Somerville estates in Scotland were on the borders of Lanarkshire and East Ayrshire and are now a suburb of Glasgow in the region of Hamilton and Motherwell. It has been suggested that the words ‘claimed to be descended from the Somervilles of Cambusnethan’ may mean that later members of the family claimed the connection. Apart from what is said above, the Cambusnethan Arms are represented on the gravestone of James the Planter’s son, Thomas, at Monea Churchyard and therefore evidence that the Planter was from the House of Cambusnethan.

One of the requirements of the Plantation was that the grantees should build strong or fortified houses or castles; apart from the fact that they were to settle themselves and their families, the structures had to be capable of protecting their families from raiding by the ‘meer’ Irish and giving cover to their livestock and men at Arms and so were likened to a garrison. It seems therefore that Tullykelter Castle was built by James the Planter shortly after 1615; while it was occupied until the early 18th century by descendants of the Planter, it is now a total ruin , indeed no more than a large pile of stones.

On 1 May, 1615, James and Elizabeth proceeded to underlet Dromscobbe to Philomy M’Cabe for 5 years and some land called Lestonier to Edmund Ballagh M’Caffrey for I year. These two tenants were ‘meer Irish, born in Ireland and by origin and race meer Irish’.. James and Elizabeth had therefore broken the conditions under which they held Dromscobbe and Lestonier so these lands were forfeited, and the King was now seised of them in fee in right of his Crown of Ireland .James and Elizabeth also demised Tullacalter to Daniel Elliot who had not taken the Oath of Allegiance. James and Elizabeth themselves, later, in 1616, took the Oath of Supremacy as required under the terms of the Plantation. (On 17th August 1616 a grant was made to… James Somervell, Esq.,…. of the Scotch nation that he be free from the yoke of Scotch or Irish servitude, and enjoy all the rights and privileges of British Subjects – Pedigree of the Earl of Erne, compiled by The Rev J H Steele 1891, p59.)

James the Planter died at Enniskillen in 1642. It is not known whether he was killed in the many skirmishes with the ‘meer’ Irish that prevailed in the 17th century, or whether he died a natural death. It is known that his will was lost or destroyed ‘by injury of war’. Nonetheless, his will was proved, presumably by reference to a copy, in…. It is not known where he was buried, He and his wife Elizabeth left 4 sons and 2 daughters.

Lady Anna Karin(Katharina) Larsdotter Grubbe Stiernfelt, was the daughter of Lord Lars Pedersson Grubbe Stiernfelt, sometime Swedish Secretary of State, and his wife Karin Gotskalksdotter. Her first husband was Ludvig Malkolmsson Hamilton through whom she had Gustav Ludvigsson Hamilton (born in late 1650s, died 1691), who became the governor of Enniskillen in Northern Ireland and 3rd Baron Deserf in the peerage of Sweden.

The two lines of the Swedish family of Hamilton stem from Malcolm Hamilton of Deserf, Archbishop of Cashel, Ireland. His sons Hugo and Ludvig entered Swedish service during the Thirty Years’ War, and in 1654 they were created Barons under the name Hamilton of Deserf. Ludvig Hamilton died in 1622, and Hugo returned home to Ireland in the same year, with the surviving family of his brother. His descendants were still living in Ireland in the late 19th century.

A third brother to Hugo and Ludvig, Captain John Hamilton, had two sons, Malcolm (1635-1699) and Hugo (1655-1724) who came to Sweden in 1654 and 1680 respectively, and were created Barons in 1689 under the name Hamilton af Hageby. The former was Major-general and Governor of Northern Sweden. The latter was made Lt.General by Charles XII and in 1715, by reason of his Scottish origin, was made commander of the planned expedition to aid the Jacobites. Malcolm Hamilton’s son, Gustaf David (1699-1788) became Field Marshal, and was created Count.
Hamiltons of both lines have played prominent roles in Swedish life right up into our own time.

The summer of 1649 saw the great historic event with which the district of Rathmines is associated, the Battle of Rathmines, resulting in the signal defeat of the Royalist Army under the command of the Marquis, afterwards Duke, of Ormonde, by the troops of the Parliament then garrisoning Dublin, under the command of Colonel Michael Jones.

It was in the immediate neighbourhood of Sir George Radcliffe's mansion on the ground now covered by Palmerston Park and the adjacent roads that Ormonde encamped his troops on moving from Finglas, where he had lingered in a state of fatal inaction for many weeks.

After the battle some of the English Royalist troops took refuge within the walls of Radcliffe's house and made so gallant a defence that it was not for some days that they laid down their arms, and then only did so on promises of safety for their lives.

Sir George Radcliffe was still stated to be owner of the lands, which included portions known as Lord Howth's land and Widow Drury's land, but his house, with a demesne of sixty acres, was forfeited and occupied by a Captain William Shore.

Captain Shore was connected with the County Fermanagh. His first wife was a daughter of Henry, Baron Dockwra, of Culmore; and Sir Henry Brooke, ancestor of the baronets of that name, who had married another daughter of Baron Dockwra, also had an interest in the house and demesne of Rathmines. On the death of his first wife, Captain Shore married the widow of Baron Lewis Hamilton, the brother of the first Lord Glenawley, and father of the distinguished defender of Enniskillen in the time of James II.

She was a native of Sweden, of which country her first husband was a noble, and is said to have been possessed of a large fortune and to have been of very high birth. She married, in addition to Baron Hamilton and Captain Shore, two other husbands, an ancestor of the Archdales of Castle Irvine,Fermanagh, and Montgomerys of Tyrone, and an ancestor of the Somerville family, now ennobled under the title of Athlumney.

Captain Shore's death occurred about 1668, and ten years later there were legal proceedings between his representatives and Thomas Radcliffe, the only son of Sir George Radcliffe, with regard to the lands of Rathmines.

Malcolm Hamilton was a Scotsman who became the Church of Ireland Archbishop of Cashel from 1623 to 1629. He was Rector of Devenish, before being appointed Chancellor of Down in 1612. He was consecrated archbishop of Cashel at Drogheda by Archbishop Christopher Hampton of Armagh on 29 June 1623. He died of a fever on 25 April 1629 and buried in the cathedral at the Rock of Cashel in County Tipperary. He had the Monea Castle built in his inherited lands in Fermanagh, starting in 1616, completed about 1618, and a bawn added in 1622.

Monea Castle is in Monea, County Fermanagh with three stories, rectangular in shape and two semi-cylindrical towers. It was built in 1618 by Malcolm Hamilton who became the Archbishop of Cashel in 1623. Gustavus Hamilton, the Governor of Enniskillen lived there until he died in 1691 with his wife and children who stayed after his death. They had to subsequently sell the estate and after a fire the castle was abandoned.

Somerville was built by Sir James Somerville, who was Lord Mayor of Dublin in 1736 and also served as MP for the city. The plan of the original house can be traced today at basement level, where a series of vaulted rooms survive with joinery details that suggest a date of c. 1730. The back of Somerville was at that time four windows wide, while the front had five.

A two-storey, stone-built stable yard lies to the north of the house. At the centre is a pedimented archway surmounted by an octagonal castellated tower. A pair of houses flanks the archway, with tripartite windows looking into the courtyard.
On the western drive, Archway Lodge is a high-rusticated arch flanked by pilasters, with substantial square rooms on either side.
The landscaped grounds include areas of protected woodland, a walled garden, and ice house.

The original St. Bride's church was an ancient Irish church located south of the walls of Dublin, dating back to pre-Viking times, and dedicated to St. Bridget (Irish: Naomh Bríd). It was located north-east of where St. Patrick's Cathedral now stands. By a grant of St. Laurence O'Toole in 1178, its revenues were appropriated to the Priory of the Holy Trinity (Christ Church Cathedral), but his was later transferred to the Economy Fund of St. Patrick's Cathedral. Until the Reformation its history was devoid of incident.

The church (now belonging to the Church of Ireland) was rebuilt in 1684 by Nathaniel Foy, rector of St. Bride's, born in York but educated in Dublin. He later became Bishop of Waterford where he founded Bishop Foy's School.

St. Bride's was closed in 1898, but its fine organ-case can still be seen in the National Museum of Ireland. It was demolished to make way for the housing development for the poor, the Iveagh Trust, financed by Edward Guinness, 1st Earl of Iveagh, which still stands on the spot.

The Hoare Baronetcy, of Annabella in the County of Cork, was created in the Baronetage of Ireland on 10 December 1784 for Joseph Hoare. He represented Askeaton in the Irish House of Commons for many years and voted against the Act of Union in 1800 at the age of over 90.
Joseph Hoare was born on 25 December 1707, the son of Edward Hoare and Grace Burton.2 He married Catherine Somerville, daughter of Sir James Somerville, 1st Bt.1 He died on 24 December 1801 aged 93.1
Joseph Hoare was from County Cork.1 He was barrister, Member of Parliament (M.P.) Askeaton, County Limerick, in 1761.1 On 10 December 1784 he was elevated to the peerage.

Public writers were corrupted without stint during the administration of Lord Buckingham. By far the ablest man in Ireland, at that day, was Dr Frederick Jebb, the Irish Junius. Under the pseudonym of Guatimozin, he published powerful letters in sustainment of his country's cause. The viceroy, writing to Lord North, says- "As the press was exceedingly violent at that time, and had greater effect in inflaming the minds of the people, it was recommended to me as a measure of absolute necessity, by some means, if possible, to check its spirit. On this a negotiation was opened with Dr Jebb, who was then chief of the political writers, and he agreed, upon the terms of my recommending him for a pension of £300 a year, to give his assistance to Government, and since that time he has been very useful, as well by suppressing inflammatory publications as by writing and other services, which he promises to continue to the extent of his power." [Memoir of Grattan, by his son, vol. ii., p. 175.] After the death of Dr Jebb the pension was continued to his children.

Among the essays published in the "Freeman," which tended to promote the Revolution of 1782, the most remarkable were those written by Dr. Frederick Jebb and Robert Johnson, under the signatures of "Guatimozin" and "Causidicus," which were several times reprinted. One of the letters of "Causidicus" contained the following passage, which has been often incorrectly quoted:- "Through the intricacies of English law the gradation of Ireland may be traced, as the way of a wounded man, by the blood which follows it."
Author of Guatimozin's letters on the present state of Ireland, and the right of binding it by British acts of Parliament.
Guatimozin (born c. 1495—died February 26, 1522), 11th and last Aztec emperor, nephew and son-in-law of Montezuma II. Also called Cuauhtemoc.

Cuauhtémoc became emperor in 1520 on the death of Montezuma’s successor, Cuitláhuac. Hernán Cortés, with powerful Indian allies, was then marching on Tenochtitlán, the Aztec capital. Cuauhtémoc’s frontier forces were forced to retreat in 1521, and he defended his capital in a four-month siege that left most of the city destroyed and few Indians surviving. Captured by the Spanish, he was at first treated with deference. Later, Cuauhtémoc was tortured to reveal the location of hidden Aztec wealth. His stoicism and refusal to speak became legendary. Fearing trouble if he left Cuauhtémoc behind, Cortés took the emperor with him to Honduras. En route, hearing of a plot against the Spaniards, he ordered Cuauhtémoc hanged. In 1949 bones purported to be Cuauhtémoc’s were discovered at Ixcateopan, Mex.

The Department of Obstetrics and Gynaecology at the Royal College of Surgeons in Ireland is one of the oldest on record, with an unbroken line of RCSI “Professors of Obstetrics and Gynaecology” (originally titled “Professors of Midwifery”) since 1770.

The discipline of obstetrics and gynaecology, arguably more than any other, has played the most major of roles in the Royal College of Surgeons in Ireland right from its very birth. The first general meeting of the College was held in the boardroom of the Rotunda Hospital on 2nd March 1784. Acknowledging that Surgeons throughout the ages practiced Midwifery, the College Charter of incorporation included a Licentiate of Midwifery. Since 1886 this has still continued to be earned by RCSI graduands as part of a conjoint diploma with the Royal College of Physicians of Ireland. In addition, since 1978, the BAO degree (Bachelor of the Art of Obstetrics) of the National University of Ireland is also awarded at undergraduate qualification.
Milestones over the past two hundred years in the RCSI Department of Obstetrics and Gynaecology include:
RCSI adopts resolution establishing “professorship of midwifery”
John Halahan, ex-assistant Master of the Rotunda becomes first RCSI Professor by introducing regular courses on midwifery
Henry Jebb, ex-assistant Master of the Rotunda replaces Halahan, and ultimately becomes President of the RCSI in 1800

profiles.name: Archibald James Somerville
profiles.file: research/David Gilmour amended records/Tranche 1/0584 ARCHIBALD JAMES SOMERVILLE(amended).doc
header: 2ND son of Capt William Somerville (0563) and Elizabeth Bellingham (0564).

fields.label: Bapt
fields.value: May 1803, at Kilkenny, by The Rev Dr Park, Lt. Campbell and Lt. Sweeney –godfathers; Miss O’B Bellingham - godmother

paras: Bapt: May 1803, at Kilkenny, by The Rev Dr Park, Lt. Campbell and Lt.
‘Archibald James born 13 May 1803, died 7 February 1871, having married twice’

It is believed AJS was the father of a child referred to in his father’s diary as ‘Little Archie’ born in1822 or early 1823 to a lady living near the Somerville family home at Cumry Lodge, Ballibay, Co Monaghan thought to be Elizabeth Breaky, daughter of James Breaky, a farmer near Cumry whom AJS subsequently married and who married a second time in 1846 and died in 1866.

AJS was also the father of 4 sons and a daughter born to a lady named Elizabeth Crawford , daughter of Jason Crawford of Oakley Park, Co Meath and Ballyholly, Co Cavan with whom he went through a marriage ceremony in 1836, but although these children were accepted as cousins by BAS(0631) and his siblings there is no primary genealogically conclusive evidence that AJS was their father.
AJS died in St Louis in 1871, in great penury, cared for by a servant girl, disowned by his sons none of whom attended his funeral

AJS seems to have been a favourite of his father, both from references in correspondence and his Diary, and from his will wherein he appointed AJS the family Executor with the family solicitor, Edward Hagarty, and left him a legacy substantially greater than that of his brothers, notwithstanding that he lived in Trinidad and had done so for many years and the evident anxiety that he had caused his parents. Furthermore, despite the difficulties of his domestic life, he was greatly loved by his siblings. He was the first of the family to go to the West Indies (1823) and subsequently to North America (1849/50).

Most of the material about AJS that survives concerns the existence of his first marriage, and, particularly, the invalidity of his second marriage to Elizabeth Crawford in 1836. No record of AJS would be complete without stating the present (2012) understanding of the material that survives.

) nee Bellingham, went to live at Cumry Lodge, Ballibay, Co Monaghan. Capt William was probably in the Louth Militia at that time. The Bellingham family had a Co Monaghan Estate near Castleblaney, Co Monaghan being the neighbouring county to Co Louth where Castle Bellingham is situated. While it is likely that Capt William and Eliza rented Cumry Lodge, their landlords were probably the Leslie Estate, rather than the Bellinghams. They remained at Cumry until about 1830/31 moving to Farm, across the county border near Galoon in Co Fermanagh, the neighbouring county
They then left that area of the country about 1835/6, moving to the north Dublin suburb of Fairview.
Much of Capt William’s Diary, which he had kept from 1811 until a few months before his death in 1844, is missing, but that for the years 1823 and 1824 is complete.

According to the Diary, on 2 February 1823, Capt William and Eliza, Bellingham Arthur, their fifth son, then aged 12, and Dorothea Riall, Eliza’s sister, left Cumry ‘about 12 o’clock at nt for Dublin on our own car, the night freezing and snowing, Bm and DR came with us. I returned home on the 19th from Dublin, while away our dear Boy went to Clonmel and remained there three days. He sailed on the 18th for Barbados in the George and Thomas.’
Before Capt William had left for Dublin on 2 February, there had been no mention of AJS leaving home.

Thereafter, from April 1823, the Diary mentions a ‘child’. Capt William and his wife arranged for the child to be put out to nurse and paid for it, and the child was occasionally brought out to Cumry, and so it went on until the end of 1824. From 5 August 1823, the child is referred to as ‘Little Archie’.
Some of the Diary entries are as follows:
7 April ‘Bartley’s woman came out with the child’
20 April ‘The nurse and child dined here’
10 May ‘Heard from Archibald from the Madeira Islands’
31 May ‘Took the child from Kitty Gorman and gave it to Scott of Ballintra’
22 June ‘Tennison rode to B.Bay to see the child’
24 June ‘Eliza and Mary went on the car to see the child’
31 July ‘E heard from D and from Archibald’
5 Aug ‘Eliza and William rode to see little Archy’
9 Nov ‘The children went on the pony and car to see Archy’
11 Nov ‘Sent the pony and car for Archy’s nurse’
17 Jan ‘Ad’s nurse here. Paid her in full to 1st of Dec 1823’
7 June ‘Eliza, Tennison and I rode to B.Bay, took Ned on Peggy with us, they rode to Nurse
8 Oct ‘Nurse Scott came here with little Archy’

The conclusion to be drawn from the unannounced departure of AJS to the Barbados and the entries in the Diary for 1823 and 1824, supported by later correspondence between the family and a Declaration made by Tenison Alan Somerville,TAS(
), shortly before his death, is that sometime in 1821
AJS cohabited with a local girl and fathered a child by her. It is also suggested that Dorothea Riall, who was close to the family and who lived near Clonmel,

privy to the affair before her sister, she having proceeded to Clonmel from Dublin in early February 1823 followed by AJS, after he had left home and before he sailed on 18 February. This is supported by Eliza receiving the two letters on 31 July 1823, one from Dorothea and one from AJS, wherein, no doubt, they revealed to Eliza all that had happened. Thereafter, Capt William names the child ‘Little Archie’.
But what had happened? In a Declaration made by TAS(
), the seventh son of Capt William and younger brother of AJS, on 14 October 1893 to his son BAS(
), who wrote it down on that day, he said as follows:

‘As regards his (Corry’s) brother Archibald James, he said that Archibald cohabited with a farmer’s daughter near Cumry, he cannot remember the name, the farmer lived on a hillside, he thinks it was called Brakey close to Cumry. The farmer had two brothers also farmers living close by. He thinks that the farmer’s daughter followed Archibald to America. They were married but he does not remember whether the ceremony took place in this country or in America, if in this country probably somewhere about Ballybay, and if in America probably at Cincinatti. This must have been about 1825. He married her before he married Elizabeth Crawford though the first wife was living and lived till long after he married Elizabeth Crawford. It was this that caused the great dissension between Archibald and Mrs Elizabeth Crawford which existed up to the time of his death.’
It had always been known in the family, as will be seen from interfamily correspondence

quoted below, that AJS had married the mother of Little Archie, but the date and place of the marriage had not been known, nor the name of the mother. TAS, in 1893, seventy years after the events he recalls
could not remember these details, but his account verifies the existence of a marriage.
As yet (2012), no entry in any Church of Ireland parish register for parishes in the vicinity of Ballibay, or Clonmel, or Dublin, ha

been found for a marriage of AJS with an unknown girl during the years 1822 or 1823. If the marriage had taken place in Ireland it would have been before 18 February 1823. Searches continue, not only in Church of Ireland Parish registers, but in Presbyterian records as well.

This failure to turn up a marriage in a parish register must be seen against the voluntary nature of registration before the Marriages Act of 1844, and the destruction of many Parish records after they were sent to the Public Records Office in Dublin
(after disestablishment of the Church of Ireland)
, which was completely destroyed by fire in the Irish Civil War of 1922.

However, recently a new lead has been found. In rural Ireland, houses and farms tend to be called after their occupants or owners, rather than their given names; so if the Jones family live at Sunny Hill, the property is customarily called
rather than Sunny Hill. There is no hillside in the vicinity of Cumry called Brakey
; but there are several families called Breaky, even now a not uncommon name in Co Monaghan. Moreover, there was a girl called Sally Breaky, working at Cumry, by whom Corry(
), AJS’ second brother, had two illegitimate daughters.

An entry in the marriage register for the Parish of Ballibay has been found for a Mrs Elizabeth Somerville, daughter of James Breaky, farmer, an illiterate lady, who described herself as a widow marrying a William Taylor, Church Sexton, widower, on 31 July 1846. AJS had left Ireland in 1823, 23 years before this marriage and his parents had left Co Monaghan more than 10 years before, so, an illiterate lady, with whom contact would long since have been lost could well imagine herself a widow.

Remember, Archibald had left in a hurry, without telling his family, so it is unlikely he would keep in touch with an illiterate girl, even though she was the mother of his child; and she, being illiterate, had no way of contacting him.
We know that the girl was of humble origin; described by Cecilia Eliza
, TAS’ wife, as a woman ‘ whose birth was so obscure that one would only rake up dirt by in any way moving in a business that must have occurred sixty years ago or more.’

A death certificate has also turned up for the same lady, then Mrs Elizabeth Taylor, wife of William Taylor, dying on 13 April 1866, aged 60 years. This would make her about 16/17 when AJS, then aged 18/19, seduced the mother of Little Archie. If it can be established that Mrs Elizabeth Taylor’s first husband was AJS, and that their marriage took place after the birth of Little Archie, as stated by TAS, then two consequences follow; firstly, Little Archie was illegitimate and, secondly, any subsequent marriage of AJS before 13 April 1866 was bigamous.
TAS said that the marriage, if in Ireland, took place probably somehere around Ballibay; if in America probably at Cincinatti. It is not known whether Little Archie’s mother accompanied AJS.
The fact that the child remains at Ballybay, with the Somervilles caring for him and paying all expenses, suggests that she left Ireland with AJS in 1823
or, as TAS says in his declaration followed him shortly afterwards

; alternatively, if the girl was really of such obscure birth and only aged 16/17 at the time, arrangements could have been made for the Somervilles to hire a nurse to assist her. Unfortunately, the passenger list for the George and Thomas is not available as the vessel was a ‘prize’ and such lists were, evidently, not retained for ‘prizes’. The girl could have sailed with AJS and, if so, the marriage could have taken place on the quayside in Dublin, where informal and unregulated marriages were performed by clerics for emigrants in those famine times, or in Madeira or Barbados. It is unlikely that the marriage took place in America, especially Cincinatti, as AJS, as far as is known, didn’t go to America until 1849/50. As far as is known, AJS never went to Cicinatti; it was his brother Corry who travelled in America
and this Declaration made by Tenison Alan had considered Corry’s affairs immediately beforehand. The old man could, momentarily, have been confused.
ful searches have been made in Madeira and Barbados; but further enquiries need to be made.
Little is known about AJS between 1823 and 1835, when he returned to see his parents, who, by that time, were living at Fairview. William Henry S
) had been sent out to Barbado
, alledgedly, to find AJS, as nothing had been heard from him since the early days of his arrival; WHS returned

, suggesting that AJS had not been found, and had probably moved on. Towards the end of this period, AJS is living and working on a sugar plantation in Trinidad and the likelihood is that he had spent most of this 12 year period in Trinidad.

Having returned to Dublin in 1835, AJS ‘married’ Elizabeth Crawford (Bessie), of Oakley Park, co Meath, Ballyholly, co Cavan and Clontarf, co Dublin; their Marriage Licence was granted on 28 November 1836 (ML Book 1835 p150, see SR 1754 L Dublin Record Office). The marriage took place on 30 November 1836, the ceremony being performed by The Rev Charles Minchin, in the Parish of Clontarf, by Consl. Licence, with the consent of their friends. The witnesses were Wm Somerville and Geo T C Smallman. GTC Smallman was the captain of a ship trading between Dublin and the West Indies and often acted as a courier for the Somerville family. The ‘condition’ of both AJS and Elizabeth Crawford was not stated in the Register; although she was described as a spinster in the Marriage Licence. The Wm Somerville who attended was Capt William. AJS’ brother, WHS,
was sent away by AJS as he would not countenance the marriage and intended to speak up. None of the Crawford family acted as a witness; it is not known whether they attended.

The following correspondence throws some light on the circumstances surrounding this second ‘marriage’ of AJS and of the implications that follow. It should be said here that although this correspondence takes place many years after the events mentioned, the events themselves,as portrayed in the correspondence, are corroborated by Capt William’s Diary, which was not known to have existed until 1899, after the death of TAS and his wife Cecilia Eliza when their house was being cleared by the family
after the death of the latter in 1898
SR 3016 E Letter dated 3 March 1879 from Eliza Nelson (Aunt Nelson) (
), Capt William and Eliza’s second daughter, who had married Thomas Nelson, written from 701 North 14th Street, St Louis, USA to Cecilia Eliza, the wife of TAS, in Dublin:

‘ The Crawfords, they lived in the Crescent, Clontarf, were never anything but hermits ………but once did I see the whole family together and that was one evening before Archibald’s sad affair. It would have been well for him if he had never met her, and he often said so. He had a wife and child, a boy 13 years old and told her so but she would not let him off -- she told her own father if he had a dozen wives she would have him. I heard John Aikens intended to look for the Ballyholly property when Jason died -- on the ground of Bessy’s children being bastards. William would not countenance the marriage and would not go. A sent him out of the way to prevent him going to the Church to forbid ….’
Note that Eliza Nelson, even though writing 43 years after the ‘marriage’ and 56 years after the birth of Little Archie , has got the age of little Archie exactly right.
SR Letter dated 18 September 1880 from Cecilia Eliza to her son BAS(
The first I heard of this business you allude to was from Aunt Nelson in Gloucester St. I did not heed it much as she was not on terms with Aunt Elizabeth(Bessie).

I then heard something of the same from Corry – they are both dead and it is not likely that anyone belonging to either could give any information. What I told you about John Eakin going to dispute Jason Crawford’s will Aunt Nelson told Papa in a letter and which letter I daresay he has somewhere – but it must have been an invention of Aunt’s for J Crawford left his first cousin John Eakin £50 and he is on the best terms with the Crawfords.

I think the girl Archibald married (if he ever did so) lived somewhere about Farm and I think I have heard Papa saying he remembered seeing a little child about the kitchen there – and that may be so - and your grandmother may have taken in his illegitimate child – as he had no home or means to do so – but do you think that if he had married that woman she would not by hook or crook have followed him to Trinidad were she his wife , believe me she would have done so, or would she have let him remain a year in Dublin without finding him out, most certainly not – or do you think your grandmother or grandfather would for the sake of her fortune connive at, or sanction by their presence at the ceremony, their son marrying a lady – knowing that their son had a wife living – for the honour of the name I hope not – Aunt Nelson told me the woman and her son were then living in New York, and that when she returned she would find them out – but she never did so- Aunt Elizabeth is now 72 – Archibald was many years in Trinidad before he came home and married Elizabeth Crawford in 1837 – is it not likely that the woman is dead – and her son also – or could it be possible that Archibald and his family could be living for several years in the same city without being found by her if she were his wife – common sense and human nature are opposed to it.

I never heard her name nor do I know what year Archibald left Ireland. Besides this woman’s birth was so obscure, that one might only rake up dirt – by in any way moving in a business that must have occurred 60 years ago or more. I have never heard of her having been in Dublin, so nothing could be known about her here – and would it not cast a blot on the children of Aunt – and do no good to anyone – but send her white head with sorrow to the grave. Ask P if he has those letters, I tell you all I know and Aunt Nelson was never proverbial for truthfulness or high principles
Ever and always your fond mother C S.’

To put Cecilia Eliza’s letter correctly in context, the girl AJS married lived near Cumry Lodge; Capt William, Eliza and family didn’t go to Farm until about 1830. Cecilia Eliza didn’t marry Tenison Alan until 1840 and then immediately afterwards went to Trinidad with Tenison Alan so she wasn’t a member of the family either in 1823 or in 1836 and, by the time she became so in 1840, her mother in law, Eliza, had died (in 1839) She therefore hadn’t had an opportunity of talking to Eliza and it is unlikely that she would have seen her letters which indicate clearly her concern about the ‘marriage’ of AJS and Bessie. She would not have known that the family had tried to stop the marriage..

Cecilia Eliza and Aunt Nelson did not get on well together and the former casts doubt on the latter’s veracity, but there is no doubt that Aunt Nelson was fully in her mother’s confidence. She was only 9 when AJS ran away, but she remembered ‘Little Archie’ and, over 40 years later, her dates were totally correct; she was also in Dublin in 1836 when AJS married Bessie and so knew all that happened then. Nothing that Aunt Nelson said has been disproved. Even a statement in a letter she wrote in 1879 describing how peculiar the Crawfords were is borne out by her mother’s letter to her 40 years earlier in which when writing of the Crawfords, she says ‘they are a curious odd family’.

In a letter dated 28 December 1838, that is two years after AJS ‘married’ Bessie, Eliza writes to her daughter Aunt Nelson at St Louis thus: “----------Indeed, I think Archd.is very careless about us all. Matrimony has completely broken all the other ties and affections of his heart. You , my darling Eliza foresaw that and told him that “if he married her, we might all bid adieu to him”. Your words have come to pass, literally – but I suppose he cannot help it, for I am certain, that three years ago, was anyone to tell him that when he married he would be quite careless and almost forsake us all, me, in particular, he would say they were mad who could ever suppose anything of the kind could ever happen”

Again, in a letter dated 3 April 1839 from Eliza to Aunt Nelson at St Louis, Eliza writes thus: “-------We have not heard from Trinidad since October, the letter I got from my darling Tenison. I think Archibald’s marriage has infuriated them all and made them lazy in the writing way. Your father and I wrote to them all by Crosby last Feby---the ‘Welcome’is expected in a week--- I have never got a letter from Archd. mentioning his child (NB his eldest child by Bessie)—in fact I have recd but three very short ones from him since he left Ireland—but we hear from Mr Bradley who you know has constant intelligence from Mr Wilson, that they are all doing well.-------"
AJS died on 7 February 1871. Correspondence suggests he was living in a garret, cared for by a servant girl, eating stir-about, neglected by his family . His sons evidently didn’t attend his funeral.
In a letter dated 6 October 1879 from Thomas Nelson at 1308,Clark Ave, St Louis (Aunt Nelson being on her deatbed, dying on 21st of that month), to Tenison Alan in Dublin, he writes as follows:

“The burden of this note is to advise you of this woman, poor Archibald’s widow (the word ‘widow’ being crossed out)—God save the mark--------I am told this woman was not the lawful wife of poor Archibald-------- The treatment she and her children gave poor Archibald at and before his death was awful---he was found dead in bed---he died for want of nourishment”

One of the interesting points about AJS and his first marriage is whether or not he and his first wife ever turned up in America. Aunt Nelson said to Cecilia Eliza, when in Dublin on a visit after her father’s death in 1844, at a time when TAS and Cecilia Eliza were living in Gloucester Street that Little Archie and his mother had been seen in New York. They would then have been about 21 and 37/38 respectively. She (Aunt Nelson) said she would make enquiries, but either didn’t or we see no evidence of the result.

Recently ( about 2009), Wendy Stevenson turned up an interesting passenger list for the ship ‘New Zealand’ sailing from ‘Great Britain, Newry Port to New York, arriving at Castle Garden (the predecessor to Ellis Island) on 2 April 1849. There were two passengers with the name Archibald James Somerville; the first one is described as ‘Sommerville,A.J.;age 30, male’ and the second as ‘Archibald J Sommerville, age 11’. The first seems a bit of a mystery; our father Archibald would have been 46, substantially more than 30. The most reasonable suggestion is that it could/would have been Little Archie; our records suggest that Little Archie was born about 1823; the passenger list suggests 1819. One always makes some allowance in the ‘age’ entry; if it had been Little Archie he would not have been with a wet nurse at the age of 3 or 4. The second entry seems to be Archibald James 2, that is AJS’ eldest son, by Bessie, who was born on 4 November 1837 which makes him 11 on 2 April 1849. Was Little Archie, then actually about 26, escorting his half brother then aged 11, who had been in Dublin with his mother (who was giving birth to her son Jason Crawford Somerville in Dublin in April 1849). If Little Archie’s mother was Elizabeth Breaky, given that she had remarried in 1846, was Little Archie emigrating to America, where his father was also now living or about to do so.

After the death of W A T B Somerville (Bunt)(0660) the eldest son of B A S(0631) in 1951 without issue, R M J B Somerville (Regi) (0670), the sole surviving son of B A S was persuaded by his youngest sisterTetty (0680), to have the details of the first marriage of AJS researched with a view to establishing, in a manner that would satisfy Garter King of Arms that he, Regi, was the then Baronet and so having himself put on the Roll. There followed about 15 years of discussions, meetings and correspondence, following detailed and lengthy research, with Sir Austin Strutt, then Registrar of the Baronetage, Sir George Bellew, then Garter King of Arms, Mr (subsequently, Sir) Walter Verco, then Chester Herald who advised generally. Regi was advised that the Pedigree should be registered and a draft was drawn up by Lancaster Herald wherein all details were approved as underlined which only left uncertainties regarding the marriages of AJS and his younger brother Corry (0586). In fact, while all other queries on the draft Pedigree were satisfactorily answered, when it went before the Chapter of the College of Arms for registration, unusually, the then Garter, Sir Anthony Wagner was present and asked that registration be deferred until he had a further opportunity of examining it. Progress was slow, apart from the fact that John (Tetty’s husband) had frequent periods of illness and eventually died in 1962 and Regi himself grew dispirited and eventually suffered from cancer and himself died in 1971.

After Regi’s death, it fell to W B R B Somerville (Bill)(0682) to persue the matter. ⟦omitted⟧ he just did not have an opportunity of taking up the necessary research himself or organising other, professional, genealogists. Eventually in the closing years of the 20th century, contact was made through a Mr Henry McDowell, a retired professional genealogist, with Mr Henry Beddingfeld in the College of Arms and some further small progress was made, but, sadly, Mr Beddingfeld lacked the interest shown in previous years by Sir Walter Verco and, following a fire in his office, retired. Further contact was made by Bill , through the Secretary of the Standing Council of the Baronetage, a Commander Perry Abbott, with Mr Peter O’Donoghue, then York Herald and a preliminary meeting held in November 2015. Mr O’Donoghue was thoroughly discouraging, maintaining that all the work and research undertaken by Regi and Tetty 50 years earlier would have to be repeated anew, the draft Pedigree prepared in the College would be ignored and any evidence from family papers would be irrelevant. He showed an amazing lack of understanding of the case and it seemed doubtful that he had even read the summary of the history provided. Since then no further action has been taken although from time to time some further information is forthcoming.

In the 2019 edition of Debretts there is an account of the descendants of AJS and Bessie, and a statement that the senior member of that line a John Somerville is the probable ninth Baronet. It is not clear who has drawn up this entry, being the first that has ever been put forward for publication in Debretts. Clearly it has been made with reference to that branch of the family as some of the information can only have been included from access to the family. At the time of the last contact with the College in 2015, it was revealed that an approach had been made to Commander Abbott, in his role of Secretary to the Standing Council, by a professional Genealogist, a Mr Stephen Kershaw, who claimed that he had ‘found’ the present Baronet in America! By coincidence the letter from Mr Kershaw arrived during the same month as Bill’s approach to Commander Abbott. By agreement with Mr Kershaw, he allowed Commander Abbott to forward to Bill his proofs which were professionally prepared but somewhat lacking in evidence. It is assumed that it is he who put forward the entry for inclusion in the 2019 edition of Debretts.

profiles.name: Elizabeth Breaky

header: Daughter of James Breaky, farmer, of Ballibay, Co Monaghan

fields.label: Married
fields.value: (1) Archibald James Somerville AJS (0584) About 1823/5; not conclusively proven. (2) William Taylor, Church Sexton, son of Edward Taylor of Ballibay; At Ballibay, Co Monaghan 31st July 1846. In the Register the wife is described as Mrs Elizabeth Somerville, a widow; she is illiterate and signs the Register with a cross.

paras: Daughter of James Breaky, farmer, of Ballibay, Co Monaghan
(2) William Taylor, Church Sexton, son of Edward Taylor of Ballibay;
At Ballibay, Co Monaghan 31st July 1846. In the Register the wife is described
as Mrs Elizabeth Somerville, a widow; she is illiterate and signs the Register

Little is known about Elizabeth Breaky for certain except the details of her second marriage and her death ; but it is known for certain that she did marry a Somerville before she married William Taylor in 1846 as the latter marriage was registered and she was then described as Mrs Elizabeth Somerville, a widow, daughter of James Breaky, farmer. There is evidence, from a Declaration made by Tenison Alan (0591) in 1893, when he was 78 years old, that his elder brother, AJS (0584), cohabited with a girl of obscure birth in 1822/3 which is corroborated by his father’s, Capt William’s (0563) diary, and that it was thought that the girl was a farmer’s daughter who lived ‘ on a hillside near Cumry’ which he, Tenison Alan,’ thought was called Brakey’. There is no such hillside. The conclusion was that the name of the girl and her father was Brakey /Breaky/Breakey as it would have been the custom in rural areas to call the farm or house by the name of the occupier; the girl’s father was a farmer and had two brothers who were also farmers. Tenison Alan went on to say that the girl, whose name he could not remember, subsequently married AJS, but he could not remember where or exactly when; he thought that if the marriage took place in Ireland it would have been in or around Co Monaghan, or if in America in Cincinnati and it was probably around 1825.Tenison Alan went on to say that the girl lived on, after the marriage to AJS, for many years and after AJS had married for the second time.

No other evidence has been forthcoming about this marriage, except in family correspondence, many years later. Searches have been made throughout Ireland for the registration of the marriage, particularly in and around Co Monaghan, in Dublin and in Clonmel, Co Tipperary where AJS’ aunt and uncle lived without success.

It is clear that at least one family called Breaky lived close to Cumry; a girl named Sally Breaky worked in the Somerville house at Cumry Lodge and had two illegitimate daughters by Corry Somerville (0586), AJS’ younger brother. There were, in fact, two families of Breaky, living in the immediate vicinity, within about 2 miles of Cumry; one at Balladian and one at Drumskelt. It is thought that the family who worked at Cumry came from Drumskelt.

A son was born to the girl in late 1822 or early 1823. The son was cared for by Capt William who arranged for nurses to care for him and paid their fees. This position continued throughout 1823 and 1824; unfortunately much of his diary for subsequent years is missing. AJS ran away from home in February 1823 when his parents were in Dublin and sailed for Barbados on 18th February 1823. There is correspondence between AJS and his mother and it seems that, by the summer of 1823, AJS has admitted that the child was his and thereafter he is named in the diary as ‘Little Archie’.

The early and secret departure of AJS so soon after the birth of the child raises the question of whether or not the mother of the child accompanied him or followed him. One would expect the mother to accompany him. Unfortunately, the ship, the ’George and Thomas’, was a prize and so no passenger list was available. However, the mother being 16 or 17, it may have been thought preferable to defer her departure until the child (and mother) were older. There is a mention in Tenison Alan’s Declaration that the mother ‘followed’ AJS; also, many years later there is a suggestion in family correspondence that both mother and child had been seen in New York, but this was not followed up at the time. If that were the case, then if as is currently believed Elizabeth Somerville was indeed the wife of AJS , she must have returned to Ireland before 1846.

paras: 4TH son of William Somerville (0563) and Elizabeth Bellingham (0564).
Birth: 19th March 1806 at Summerville, Carrick on Suir, Co Tipperary
Bapt: 6th April 1806 at Carrick on Suir. Godparents: James Corry Esq.,Miss Briscoe of Tenvane.
Buried: Woodland Cemetery, Cleveland. Burial recorded as Conrad Sommerville;Vault located Sec 24. lot 89.

Notes: For many years there was a mystery as to whether Corry was married or not. In correspondence with his family after he had emigrated to Canada, and from his behaviour before that, the signs were that he hadn’t married. He never mentioned a wife although it was clear that he had children.

Corry wrote a charming letter(in a beautiful hand) on 1st July 1857 from Canada to his brother Tenison Alan (0591) in Dublin in which he mentions his children as Eliza, Margaret Adelaide, William Bellingham, Dorothea Victoria, Henrietta Alicia and Lucinda Catherine, all of whom were being cared for by others. There is no mention of a mother to his children, nor of a wife. In fact, he says at the end “I have now no-one to provide for but myself.”

He had emigrated in 1834 and while there was a suggestion that he married in 1830, he continued to have illegitimate children up to 1833 at which time he was still living at home. These children were Sally daughter of Sally Breaky, bapt. 27th Jany 1826 ,Matilda daughter of Sally Breaky, bapt.2nd Sept.1827, Mary Jane daughter of Mary Cunningham bapt.5th April 1833.The above baptisms were entered, and the illegitimacy noted, in the Register of Aughnamullen Church in the Parish in which Cumry was situated. Sally Breaky worked in the house at Cumry, while Mary Cunningham’s brother was a schoolteacher at Cumry. There is also evidence that Sally had a 3rd child by someone else and then went to Belfast, while Mary Cunningham had 2 illegitimate boys by Corry, one of whom became a Police Constable in Northern Ireland.

Eliza Nelson (0596), in a letter to Tenison Alan, said Lucinda Simonton(0587) who had worked at Farm, was the mother of Corry’s children, but there was no mention of a marriage. Searches in parish registers in Dublin and around Co Monaghan produced no evidence, and nothing was forthcoming in America.

About 2006, WBRBS received a letter from a Mrs Wendy Stevenson in Canada, addressed to William Somerville, co Meath, Ireland asking whether he was, in anyway, connected to this Somerville family. It turned out that Mrs Stevenson is married to a descendant of Dorothea Victoria, daughter of Corry. Her husband, Robert, has what she calls the Canadian edition of the Family Bible which records a marriage of Corry and Lucinda Simonton in 1834, but there is no further evidence as to where such a marriage might have taken place. In the Irish(original) Family Bible, no marriage is recorded.

There was a further suggestion of a marriage. Corry came to Dublin in 1874 and left a pedigree showing a marriage between himself and Lucinda in 1830, but no details. Subsequently the Cleveland Leader of 28th January 1875 published an obituary of the death of Lucinda,’wife’ of Corry, on 25th January that year. Corry wrote to Tenison Alan on 9th June 1875 and specifically mentions his wife for the first time, saying how he has aged since the ‘departure of my dearly beloved wife.’

Eventually, as the issue of this marriage remained unresolved, further searches were made and WBRBS was able to turn up an entry for a marriage between Corry Somerville and Lucinda Simonton (the names being somewhat ‘garbled’) for 16th Sept 1834 in the private manuscript Register of the Rev J.G.F.Schulze, at the Lutheran Church, Poolbeg Street, Dublin, that is to say ‘on the quay side’. In the 18th and early 19th centuries, when there was substantial emigration from Ireland to the New World, groups of pastors, belonging mainly to reformed continental Churches, were licensed to perform marriage ceremonies between couples among their own flock who were emigrating ,or wanted privacy and, therefore wished to avoid banns, or entering into marriages of which their families disapproved or who couldn’t afford the costs of a regular ceremony. The pastors themselves became known as ‘Couple Beggars.’ The ceremony was often celebrated in a private house and the witnesses provided by the pastor himself. Informal records were kept by the pastor. Unfortunately nearly all these private records have been lost or destroyed in the Four Courts fire, save two Registers of Mr Schulze which luckily cover the year 1834. While the pastors were licensed to celebrate the marriages for their own flock, they actually exceeded their authority, no doubt for a fee; the number of such pastors was substantial and the marriages numbered many thousands. The validity of the marriages has been successfully tested and upheld in the Courts.

The thought has not escaped the writer that Corry was introduced to the idea of using a Couple Beggar by his elder brother, AJS, who was perhaps marrying a girl of whom his parents would have disapproved in exactly the same way ,ie immediately before emigration, only 11 years before.

Corry and Lucinda arrived in New York, destined for Upper Canada, on 8th November 1834 in the ship ‘Ocean.’ Initially, they settled in Rochester, New York. Their eldest daughter Eliza was born there on 28th February 1835 and their second daughter Margaret Adelaide on 14th February 1836. At this time there was unrest in Canada, leading up to the Rebellion in 1837. Corry’s maternal second cousin Capt William Bellingham had a company of militia at Toronto. Corry’s mother, Eliza, writes to her daughter, Eliza, Corry’s sister, on 14th June 1839 …” I received a long letter from your dear brother Corry about a fortnight after I wrote last to you, 4th April, he was in excellent health and had joined the Army, a Volunteer, and was to have got his commission on ? May. He has made many good and respectable friends at Toronto where he is quartered, and in case the country becomes quiet and the Military is disbanded, he has very good prospects of getting a good civil situation. Do you remember little William Bellingham, at Aunt Alley’s, a very handsome boy, the youngest son of my cousin Fitzalan and brother of Sir Edward, who you saw with me in D’Olier Street. – He is a lawyer and has a company of militia at Toronto- and Corry almost lives with him and he has introduced him to all the Respectable Society there – and Corry still expects to hear from you in reply to his letter, he always writes very affectly about you, he is greatly vexed and no wonder with all his brothers in Trinidad , at never having received one from any of them- it is very provoking” His mother Eliza didn’t mention that Corry and Lucinda had recently delivered their son William Bellingham on 28th April 1839 in Toronto. Perhaps Corry had not mentioned it to her.

It appears that the commission and the civil appointment didn’t work out, as by the New York census of 1840, Corry and his family were living back in Rochester where he was a Station Agent. Dorothea Victoria was born there on 24th September 1840, Henrietta Alicia on 18th May 1844 and Lucinda Catherine on 4th January 1846.

Corry seemed to be a restless soul, always looking for something different and better, continuing to change residences and employment .In 1844, when Lucinda was born, he was a carpenter, living at 54, Water Street, Rochester; in 1845 a carpenter and joiner living at 81, North Clinton Street, Rochester. By 1847 he was living at 38, Atwater Street, Rochester. Records show that by 1848, he and his family had gone to Canada and were farming at Caistor, Lincoln Twp, Ontario. The 1851 census shows him living in Caistor Twp on a farm between John Gamble and the Dennis family.. His eldest daughter married John Gamble and his second daughter married Sinicoe Dennis. Corry appeared to work hard physically and claimed to hold many civic offices although there are no records of him holding these offices, but within 4 years he became ill with some kind of infection in his foot which debilitated him both physically and emotionally and drained his resources. It was 4 years before he recovered and during that period he was ‘unavailable’ to his family.

In a letter of 1st July 1857 to his brother Tenison, Corry mentioned that he had not heard from Tenison since May 1841. Corry said that, in the meantime, he had got into a lucrative business “and as the saying goes, made money like dirt, and in about 6 years had quite a respectable sum saved and came over to Canada and bought a lot of land, 114 acres, and commenced cleaning a place for a house and got a very handsome house up and good offices etc, and in (18)52had about 60 acres cleared and was just going ahead. I held many situations here, while on my farm; overseer of highways- District, County and Township, School Superintendent, Township Clerk, Auditor of Public Acts, Township Councillor – Justice of Peace, etc ,etc. but the salaries attached to offices in this country are small, very small indeed- all the fat you would raise off them you might blow through a humming bird’s quill in a mosquito’s eye- and it would’nt wink- however taking farming, and all together I would by this time have been (if not wealthy) comfortably independent- but the great disposer of all events saw fit to order otherwise. I suppose there was too much dross in the gold and I had to pass through the furnace of affliction, and a hot fire it has been- however I hope the gold is fine- over 4 years I took some kind of disease in one of my feet and never left my bed except to have it made for more than 2 years and was then on crutches for 2 years more. I went to New York in July 55 (then on crutches) to get the benefit of the sea water and medical advice having tried all the M.Ds here who gave it as their opinion there was no way of saving my life except amputation of the limb. I saw Archibald wife and family, Archd. left, a few days after I arrived, for St Louis. I have since heard all the family are there. I hear sometimes from A, last about 6 months since. Eliza and I used to correspond very regularly- but all at once it stopped and I have not had a line from her in two years, for what reason I am unable to say- perhaps the thought I might become ? had one of my little daughters with me. Mrs McDonnell(Sister in law Henrietta, widow of brother William who died at sea in 1847) acted ridiculous- but more and much of all these things some other time – what with the lack of faithful persons to attend to my affairs, the expense of a family and the large expense of professional attendants- and the conduct of some, was used up in means. And all these combined with my long illness completely prostrated not only my physical, but mental powers, reason was for a long time gone. A few months ago, I (as it were) woke out of a long sleep. I am now well., never was in better health and my foot is almost well. I will soon be ready for business again, what I will do I am not decided upon yet. I am in a light situation in this place, the salary is small, 100 pounds Halifax, c. 400 a year (Corry was Station Master at Welland, Ontario and the family had obviously moved from the farm in Caistor). The two letters you mention to have written never found me and hard for them to do so, as I have not been in Toronto to live since 39. Elizabeth could not give me your address more than Dublin which as you say is no address at all. Had I known your whereabouts I should have written to you then, and often since – but we must make up for lost time, and when you are so busy as not to have time, I will expect Dear Sister to do so and will look for her letters at any rate. You do not tell me how many little ones you have, consequently do not know how well off you are. I count every one a thousand pounds at interest. You are right, I have grandchildren, four of them - that I know of.”
Corry, in his letter of 1st July 1857 goes on to describe his 6 children as follows:
….”No 1 Elisa, a Bellingham- black eyes and black hair, fair skin, considered pretty, married to John Gamble, a red hot Otrangeman from the black north, a good farmer.

No 2 Margaret Adelaide ‘soft blue eyes’ very fair, a good deal of Mother’s sweetness and her figure, married to Sinicoe Dennis, a good natured Dutchman does not know any better than to treat her as well as his horses – and they are always fat – a big farmer.
No 3 William Bellingham, the ditto of yourself, fair hair and blue eyes, a big good natured fellow and smart withal.
No 4Dorothea Victoria, black hair, black eyes and skin of the same colour and considered very clever and very handsome. I will say very good and hard work to prevent her from being taken away.
No 5 Henrietta Alicia it is thought will eclipse them all – very like myself – not fully developed yet
No 6 Lucinda Catherine, a pretty little curly ?, all fair – a pair of little devils stuck in her head which I fear will do mischief – let those who would be safe keep out of her way.”
Corry goes on to say that the two youngest are with each of their married sisters, and Dorothea was away visiting a lady friend in Rochester, and William is with one or the other of his brothers in

law, so “I am all alone so far as my own family is concerned”. At one point, Corry asked his sister Eliza to take in his son William and give him an education with a view to getting a good appointment. This may have lead to a temporary estrangement between them.
The census of 1861 shows Corry and Lucinda living in Welland with Dorothea and William; Corry was a station agent, William a telegraph operator and Dorothea ‘at home’

Corry’s obituary says that the family stayed for a time in Buffalo and Cincinnatti before moving to Cleveland in 1864. Meanwhile, the American Civil War was raging; William had joined the Union Army . Corry lived at 4 different places in Cleveland before the 1870 census; he was a produce and commission merchant at 72 Merwin Street with ‘Shotter and Somerville’.

By the census of 1870, Corry had given up his business and was in the hospitality industry, as he and Lucinda are keeping a hotel at 911 Broadway in Cleveland. Also living there were Dorothea and her husband Hugh Stevenson, who were married in January 1869. Maggie (Somerville)Dennis and her husband were also living in the hotel.

Corry became a naturalised citizen of the U.S.A. on 25 March 1874. Later that year, on 16 September 1874 he sent a pedigree of his family to his brother Tenison Alan Somerville, showing that his son William Bellingham was born on 28 April 1839 and that he married Amanthus, daughter of Ewell Shipp of Kentucky on 1 August 1867 and then had no issue. In the letter Corry says that ‘Lucinda Catherine had 5 children – 3 living – and one son my William Bellingham – the prospects are that my line will become extinct through him – as God pleases’. By now, Corry was living at 706, Broadway Cleveland where he was a Telegraph Operator , at age 69. Lucinda died there on 25 January, 1875 and was buried on 28 January in Vault 75, Woodlawn Cemetery, Cleveland.

Corry made a trip to Ireland in 1874 and after his return was living with his daughter Maggie and her family on Independence Street, Cleveland. He died there on 12 January 1879 from inflammation of the bowel and was buried in Woodland Cemetery S24L89, Cleveland. The cemetery record shows him as Conrad Sommerville, buried in Vault, Sec24, Lot89.

Subject: Obituary for Lucinda SOMERVILLE, b. Co. Fermanagh 1806, d. Cleveland 1/25/1875 Date: Sun, 3 Aug 2003 13:51:58 -0400

“Among my papers I have just found a lengthy "memorial" for "Lucinda Somerville, beloved wife of Corry Somerville, eldest daughter of Thomas Simonton, Esq., and Margaret Shaw of County Fermanagh." She married Corry Somerville in 1834 and emigrated to Rochester, N.Y. the same year. They moved to Cleveland in 1864 and she died there January 25, 1875. It is a copy of a newspaper article which I suspect I copied for someone on this list several years ago, when I was reading microfilm of the Cleveland newspapers. I am not related to this person, but if any of you happen to be related or know someone who is, let me know and I will send the article.” Janet Friend
E-mail sent to Janet Friend on 2 Jul 2011 explaining that Corry Somerville’s younger brother
was my great-great grandfather. No response to date (30 July 2011). DRG Gilmour.

There has been a suggestion among Somerville papers that Thomas Simonton was a preacher or clergyman, and that he came from Monaghan Town, but no firm evidence is forthcoming. Following from the obituary put in the newspaper by Corry after her death, Lucinda was the daughter of Thomas Simonton, Esq. and Margaret Shaw. Descended paternally from a ‘good old Protestant family in Scotland, many of whom were in the ministry of the Protestant Episcopal Church of England. Her mother was connected with the first Wesleyan Methodists.’

Lucy and George Kerr had two sons, Robert and John; but their father emigrated to America in 1827, leaving Lucy and the two boys in Ireland. George then died in America before he was able to return to collect his family. Lucy then started working in the Somerville house, possibly before they left Cumry Lodge, but certainly when they were at Farm. When Corry married Lucy in 1834, they went to America immediately afterwards and initially lived in Rochester,NY. There is no further mention of Robert and John, but no suggestion that they emigrated with Lucy and Corry. It is not known whether Robert and John stayed with George’s parents or with Lucy’s. Lucy seems to have abandoned any responsibility for them.
Lucy was the mother of the following children by Corry:
Margaret Adelaide, born 14th Feby 1836, Rochester, NY.
William Bellingham, born 28th April, 1839, Toronto, Upper Canada.

Corry and Lucy were confirmed on 8th Aug 1837 and 16th Feby 1848 respectively at St Paul’s Episcopal Church, Rochester.The children were all baptized there 1st March 1844, except Lucinda Catharine who was sick and baptized privately at home Atwater Street,16th Aug 1847, by JV VanIngen.
Lucy is not mentioned in Corry’s letters to members of his family until after her death on 25th Jany 1875.

Among my papers I have just found a lengthy "memorial" for "Lucinda Somerville, beloved wife of Corry Somerville, eldest daughter of Thomas Simonton, Esq., and Margaret Shaw of County Fermanagh." She married Corry Somerville in 1834 and emigrated to Rochester, N.Y. the same year. They moved to Cleveland in 1864 and she died there January 25, 1875. It is a copy of a newspaper article which I suspect I copied for someone on this list several years ago, when I was reading microfilm of the Cleveland newspapers. I am not related to this person, but if any of you happen to be related or know someone who is, let me know and I will send the article. Janet Friend
E-mail sent to Janet Friend on 2 Jul 2011 explaining that Corry Somerville’s younger brother
was my great-great grandfather. No response to date (30 July 2011). DRG Gilmour.
There has been a suggestion among Somerville papers that Thomas Simonton was a preacher or clergyman, and that he came from Monaghan Town, but no firm evidence is forthcoming.

Following from Obit, put in newspaper by Corry on her death: Lucinda was eldest daughter of Thomas Simonton, Esq and Margaret Shaw. Descended paternally from 'a good old Protestant family in Scotland, many of whom were in the ministry of the Protestant Episcopal Church of England. Her mother was connected with the first Wesleyan Methodists. George Kerr's fatherr was a Wesleyan preacher.

Lucy and George Kerr had two sons, Robert and John; but their father emigrated to America in 1827, leaving Lucy and the two boys in Ireland. George then died in America before he was able to return to collect his family. It isn’t certain that he had plans to return for Lucy and his sons, perhaps he wanted a ‘new life’. As there is no further knowledge of the 2 sons, it is unknown at this point if they stayed with George’s parents or Lucy’s. She certainly appears to have abandoned responsibility for them. Lucy then started working in the Somerville house, possibly before they left Cumry Lodge, but certainly when they were at Farm. When Corry married Lucy in 1834, they went to America immediately afterwards and initially lived in Rochester,NY. There is no further mention of Robert and John, but no suggestion that they emigrated with Lucy and Corry.
Lucy was the mother of the following children by Corry:
Margaret Adelaide, born 14th Feby 1836, Rochester, NY.
William Bellingham, born 28th April, 1839, Toronto, Upper Canada.

Corry and Lucy were confirmed on 8th Aug 1837 and 16th Feby 1848 respectively at St Paul’s Episcopal Church, Rochester.The children were all baptized there 1st March 1844, except Lucinda Catharine who was sick and baptized privately at home Atwater Street,16th Aug 1847, by JV VanIngen.
Lucy is not mentioned in Corry’s letters to members of his family until after her death on 25th Jany 1875. Buried in Woodland Cemetery, Cleveland. Sec 24, Lot 89 - Vault 75 3/31/1875; ‘used again’
