header: Of Louisville Kentucky; originally from Virginia.
Father of Amanthus Shipp (0614).
paras: Of Louisville Kentucky; originally from Virginia.
Notes: Ewell Shipp and his wife were wealthy plantation owners, having been awarded land in
Source: Somerville Index and Wendy Stevenson.
SHIPP FAMILY IN THE AMERICAS – to Ewell Shipp and his daughter Amanthus Shipp who married William Bellingham Somerville

There are several Shipp ‘histories’ that claim that William Shipp, from England, was the first Shipp to settle in early 1600’s in Rappahanock County, Virginia. (Sanders) He was appointed by the General Assembly as a viewer of the tobacco crop of 1639, and a vestryman in the colonial church. He died in 1657 and left a son, Josiah Shipp. (Virkus) It is quite possible that this is the Josiah Shipp who is ancestor to Amanthus Shipp, however, it is possible that this is not the same Josiah Shipp for whom we have documented links.

On May 3, 1688, the Rappahannock County Court issued a “Certificate according to act of Assembly is granted to Joseph Buckley and Mary Buckley for two hundred and fifty acres of land due for the importation of five persons by name: Francis James, Josiah Ship, John Manning, Joseph Beckley and Mary Beckley.”

In early Colonial days, a person could receive a patent of 50 acres of land for each person they imported to America, many of these new arrivals being indentured servants, who sold themselves into servitude in order to reach the Colonies. So, if Joseph Buckley is ‘importing’ Josiah Shipp, or ‘claiming’ that he did, as well as claiming lands for himself, then Josiah could not have already been in the colony and a son of William Shipp who was already here. It is possible that William and Josiah were related, or ‘crafty’ in their claims, but there isn’t definitive proof of parentage. It was also common for claimants of the patents to wait as long as 15 years before making the claim, so Josiah Shipp could have arrived in mid 1670’s. From later records, we know that he was a cooper, a trade that he could have learned in England, or in the colonies. Vol. 16 of the Virginia Colonial Abstracts Deed Book shows Josiah Shipp purchasing 100 acres on the north side of the Rappahannock River from the same Joseph Beckley for 3,000 pounds of tobacco and casks in March of 1692 (Early Colonial Settlers). Apparently ‘importers’ often sold land to the importees. It is also possible that there was some manipulation, given the ongoing financial relationship between Josiah Shipp and Joseph Buckley, and that Josiah was, indeed, the son of William of Rappahannock. The reason for detail of Josiah’s land ownings is to show how he came into possession of ‘my plantations’, whether as a cooper or as a lawyer, and that the Shipp family had funds that would allow them to buy land 100 years later in Kentucky. While some of the Shipp sons did serve in the Revolutionary War, and probably the French and Indian Wars, there doesn’t appear to be any evidence to support large land grants for these reasons. That is not to say that it didn’t happen, but it is dubious to make that claim without support.

On August 1, 1685, Francis Triplett and Samuel Bowen of Sittingburn Parish, Rappahannock Co. conveyed to Josiah Shipp 1050 acres on the North Side of the Rappahannock River (later Richmond County and the south side of the river became Essex County), which had been granted to Triplet in 1660. It is unclear what happened to the bulk of the land, but in 1695, Thomas Meader deeded to Josiah Shipp 150 acres of land ‘whereon the said Josiah Shipp now lives’ in County of Essex, Parish of Sittinburn, for the ‘valuable consideration of Four Thousand pounds of tobacco and cask”. Josiah was said to have 350 acres in the 1704 quitrent list. This likely included the 150 acres he lived on in Sittingburn, the land that Triplett and Bowen conveyed to him in 1685, and the 100 acres he purchased from Beckleys in 1692. If this assumption is correct, then he got 100 acres from Triplett and Bowen.

Josiah Shipp was resident in St. Anne’s Parish, Rappahannock Co (now Essex Co) from at least 8 November 1673 when he was referred to in a document by Bray as ‘my loving friend and lawyer’ (Tyler). So, we know that Josiah was possibly a lawyer, but later documents suggest that he was a cooper, and that the Bray and Shipp families were well acquainted from at least that time. In order for him to witness documents, Josiah would be at least legal age of 21, therefore born before 1652, contrary to many claims that he was born in 1664. Josiah Shipp married Elizabeth Brookes, daughter of wealthy landowner Thomas Brookes and Susannah Wyatt in Rappahannock Co., Virginia. Given the date of birth of their first child, they would have married circa 1650, which makes Josiah born circa 1630 – certainly not in 1664 as often claimed. The name Wyatt shows up in future generations as a forename.

On July 2, 1695, Josiah and Elizabeth were living on a 150 acre plot of land in Sittingburne Parish in Essex County, so he was on the south side of the river at that time. In 1704, Josiah petitioned the House of Burgesses for permission to keep a ferry on the Rappahannock River, as he was ‘aged and unable to do other work”. Again, as many sources claim that Josiah was born in 1664, this cannot be correct, as he would not have been ‘aged’ in 1704. He had to have been born before 1652, as previously stated. Apparently, Elizabeth died, and Josiah remarried to Jane, as she is mentioned in his will of 24 January 1705, proved 12 February 1705. Josiah left a considerable estate in goods and chattels to his three sons, Richard, Josiah, and Thomas but to his eldest, Richard, he left “my plantation with all ye land appurtenances and privileges thereunto”.
Josiah, born before 1650, and Elizabeth Brookes Shipp had issue:

i Richard, born in 1670, died bef May 19, 1724 when his will was proved, in Parish of St. Anne, Essex Co., Virginia, probably still living on the land left to him by his father, Josiah. Essex Co. became Spottsylvania Co in 1720. Richard Sr. married Mary and had 2 sons. Richard left his lands, after the death of his wife, Mary, to his son, Thomas, who was probably the elder son. He also left his negro woman, Sukey. Issue of Richard and Mary
A Thomas, born bef 1702, married Elizabeth ? about 1723,died 1752
in Caroline Co., Virginia. Thomas and Elizabeth and Richard removed to Orange Co., then Caroline Co., Virginia, where Thomas died in 1752. Thomas and Elizabeth had issue:
i Richard, born 1725 in St. Anne’s Parish, Essex Co.

Richard died in 1781 in Culpepper Co., Virginia. He served in the Revolutionary War and was a Private in General Nelson’s Corps of Light Dragoons. Richard married first, Elizabeth in about 1755 and had by her:

Thomas’ wife, Elizabeth died, and Richard married secondly to Isobel, to whom he left his estate in 1781. In 1784 (Sanders), widowed Isobel and (step) sons Ambrose, Richard, John and Thomas removed to Greene County, Kentucky, where it appears that her nephew Richard had settled some three years previously in 1781. Isobel and the sons settled on farms near present day Campbellsville, near Salome.

ii Thomas, born c 1727 in Essex Co, and died in 1776 in Caroline County. Like his brother Richard, Thomas the younger also served as a Private in the Revolutionary War but as he died in 1776, one wonders if it was a consequence of injuries or disease suffered during the war. Thomas married Rachel Grant, in about 1746, and had issue, 9 children (more follows):

B Richard, born 1703. This Richard could be the progenitor of John, born c 1725, who was father to Richard Wyatt, Laban and Colby Shipp who were part of the Travelling Church (discussed later) that migrated to Kentucky in 1784. The brothers received massive land grants of over 29,000 acres near Georgetown, Kentucky.

ii Josiah, son of Josiah, born Essex County, 1672, married Elizabeth Hodgson. On August 16, 1715, John and Elizabeth Hodgson of St. Anne Parish, Essex Co., gifted to Josiah and their daughter Elizabeth ‘all the land in which they now live in a swamp called Long Bridge, being 30 acres’. This deed was witnessed by Richard Shipp, probably Josiah’s brother.
iii Thomas, third child of Josiah Sr., was born c. 1674 in Essex Co. He married Elizabeth ____, removed to Orange Co., Virginia and died there c. 1746.
Generation 6 continues with children of Thomas SHIPP and Rachel Grant. (Thomas was the son of Thomas and Elizabeth, and great-grandson of Josiah and Elizabeth Brookes SHIPP):

Richard Jonathan Shipp, born November 12, 1747 (married Elizabeth Doniphan in King and Queen Co., Virginia on February 1774). Richard was a Private in General Nelson’s Corps of Light Dragoons stationed at Baltimore on July 29, 1778. His brother Lemuel was in the same Corps. Richard died 1821 (more follows)
i Mary, born November 1774, married John Shepherd August 27, 1795 in Woodford Co., KY
ii Elizabeth D, born August 1776, died c. 1805, married Obadiah Fogg
iv Richard D., born October 14, 1779, died February 12, 1852, buried on Shipp farm at Sunny Slope, married Sarah McCracken December 23, 1802. He was cabinet maker and contractor, and had 9 children:
John G., born October 21, 1820, cabinet maker.
Thomas H., born September 23, 1824, married Mary Van de Gref
v Narcissus, born June 1781, married Rev. John Edwards
vi Sophia, born June 1785, married Laban Sebree
vii Son, born March 15, 1783, lived only a few days

viii Emma Grant Shipp, born October 29, 1787, married William Truman August 27, 1807, Woodford Co., KY (he was born January 15, 1783). They had 11 children, the fifth of whom was Anderson Shipp Truman, born February 27, 1816, and who was the father of US President Harry S Truman
x Anderson Doniphan Shipp, born November 15, 1792, married Elizabeth Blanton and had 7 children
xi John G. Shipp, born August 12, 1779 (or 1775 in another source), died February 12, 1877 on Sunny Slope Farm, unmarried, cabinet maker and contractor

Meanwhile the Revolutionary War had ended, and the country was recovering. Both sons of Thomas and Elizabeth had died, Richard in 1776 and Thomas in 1781. While the Shipp families lived in St. Mary’s Parish, it is not clear if this was a geographic term, or an English established Church Parish. Certainly the family had attended the colonial church. Nevertheless it is known that some membes of the Shipp family were part of “The Travelling Church”. Seeking religious freedom and economic opportunity, in 1781 Rev Lewis Craig led a group numbering about 600 people, the majority of whom were Baptists,and part of Lewis’ Upper Spottsylvania Church, along with other settlers joining in. They were leaving behind the discrimination they felt from the established church in colonial Virginia, and they sought fertile soil for both physical and spiritual fruitbearing. It is not clear if the Shipps were part of the Baptist congregation, as they had belonged to the established colonial church, but there were certainly many later Shipps involved in the Baptist churches in Kentucky.

According to descendent Sanders, Richard and Elizabeth and their children and families moved with “The Travelling Church” to Kentucky in 1784, where they settled on vast land grants. This is not accurate, as in her biography, Emma Shipp Truman, their 8th child was born in 1787 in St. Mary’s Parish, Caroline Co. Virginia, and says that she came with her parents to Woodford Co., Kentucky when she was six, therefore in 1793. Richard’s brother Edmund came the same year, and brother Ewell came around the same time.

In 1784, and probably with the Travelling Church came brothers Richard Wyatt Shipp, Laban Shipp. A third brother Colby Shipp came about the same time, perhaps a little later. These brothers were the sons of John

Shipp, born about 1725, married to Sally Johnson. Richard was born April 26, 1750 and Laban was born 1757. They were both executors of their father’s will. Sanders claims that John, born c. 1725 is a son of Thomas and Rachel, but this is not biologically possible. There is no doubt that they are some connection, but not as indicated by Sanders. John is more likely the son of Richard (B above, born 1703), or a son of ii Josiah or iii Thomas

From 1794, Richard Shipp is listed on the tax rolls of Woodford Co. until 1828, when he died. He was also listed in Shelby Co., KY. As Emma stated that she came to Woodford Co. with her father when she was 6, it means that the family came in 1793, and not 1784 as claimed by Sanders. Brothers Edmund and Richard Jonathan and Ewell all moved to Kentucky in approximately 1793. Richard left behind his three oldest daughters who were under 21 and chose guardians for when they remained in Virginia. Mary and Narcissus later removed to Woodford Co., KY, as did Elizabeth , but she died soon after and her husband, Obadiah Fogg, returned to King and Queen County, Virginia.

Richard and Elizabeth acquired 168 acres, probably in 1793, which they called Sunny Slope Farm, made up of luxurious pastures on the Aiken Road near Midway, Woodford County, Kentucky. Originally the family lived in a cabin on the land while they were building their home. Brothers Richard D. and John G. Shipp, the sons of Richard and Elizabeth, settlers from Caroline County, Virginia built a handsome one and a half story house at Sunny Slope in 1820 near the site of their parent's cabin. All the brick and lumber for the house came from their farm. The Shipps were known as both builder/carpenters and furniture makers.
In early 20th century the Shipps were dealers in tobacco seed, and also bred race horses. A description of the house follows.

The second son of Thomas and Rachel Shipp, Edmund, married Tabitha Garnett. In 1780 Edmund Shipp shows up in Tax Records of Caroline County, Port Royal, Virginia, owning 6 slaves. Edmund Shipp owned 445 acres of land in Caroline County, which he sold before moving to Kentucky in 1794.
Edmund and Tabitha had eight children named in his will:
Ewell was born shortly before the family’s arrival in Jefferson Co., Kentucky. Ewell married Evalina Bray in Nov 1, 1821, and had issue:
Amanthus Shipp, born December 8, 1825. More follows.
Amelia Shipp, born March 1827, married William Hastings
Adelia M. Shipp, born 1829, married Thomas E. Browne Jr (he born 1824)

5 Samuel B Shipp, born 1833, married Nannie R ___ (born 1850), and they had issue: James W (1868), Adelia (1870), Edmund (1874) and Ewell (1876). In 1880, Samuel and Nannie lived in Spring Garden, Jefferson Co., KY, and had 2 domestic staff and 4 men who worked on the farm. All were ‘black’ or ‘mulatto’.
It should be noted that the Garnett and Bray families were close friends and neighbours of the Shipp families that resided on plantations in Virginia.

Ewell Shipp’s farm was located where the University of Illinois is now. Shipp Street would be almost in the middle of the campus (From A Centennial History of the University of Louisville ln google books, p. 65. Lying within one of the early tracts identified in the Fincastle surveys of 1774, which rewarded Virginia veterans of the French and Indian Wars, the land that became this new Third Street eventually was owned by Ewell Shipp. His heirs sold the land to Thomas Browne, who in turn sold 82.5 acres to the city of Louisville for about $10,000 in 1850. It was specified by Browne that the land be used for the benefit of the public. This property was occasionally referred to as the "Southern Cemetery" and was known legally as the Oakland Cemetery, although there is no evidence that anyone was ever buried there. Shipp Street, for many years the northern border of the campus, was named for Ewell Shipp (p. 68). Bullitt & Shipp held a cotton partnership in 1851-52, but it is uncertain which Shipps were the partners.

Ewell Shipp left large inheritances to his children. In 1850 Amanthus was worth $10,000 (today’s inflated value would be $338,000, according to Measuring Worth) and her heirs continued to receive royalties from an oil company on land in Catron Creek, Kentucky, until at least 1941.

Amanthus Shipp married Leander Buckner June 23, 1846. He died 22 November 1855; buried Cave Hill Cemetery, Louisville, Kentucky. By him she had three sons: Ewell S Buckner, born 1847; William Henry Buckner, born 1848 and died December 30, 1852; and Edmund Garnett Buckner, born September 8, 1850.

Amanthus Shipp Buckner married, secondly, William Bellingham Somerville on August 1,1868. He had been a Colonel in the Telegraph Service of the Union Army during the Civil War. Amanthus’ brother had served in the Confederate Army. That must have meant for interesting dinner time conversation! William died April 24, 1897 and was buried April 28, 1897 in Woodland Cemetery, Cleveland, near his parents. Amanthus died October 26, 1906 in Kirkwood, Missouri, and was buried October 27, 1906 in Cave Hill Cemetery, Louisville, Kentucky, near her first husband and son William Buckner.
(continuing children of Thomas and Rachel Grant Shipp)

3 Gideon, born 1756 He resided in Essex Coounty, where he married Mrs. Alice (Dunn), Emmerson, daughter of William Dunn, and widow of James Emmerson, of Essex. On 2 July 1790 Gideon Shipp, in a very courtly hand, penned a letter to Captain James Edmondson praying he would stop the sale of the said Shipp’s personal property to satisfy a certain judgement. Gideon Shipp died in Essex County prior to 14 June 1797, when his four children, Alice, Katy, Thomas and Ann Shipp, had
4 Ann Ann Shipp, born in Caroline County circa 1755, married James Garnett; they moved to Woodford County, Kentucky. In a deposition made

in Woodford County 6 October 1806 James Garnett deposes in a suit relative to the estate of Lemuel Shipp of Caroline County, VA deceased, in which he states that he was well acquainted with the very handsome personal estate possessed by Lemuel Shipp, having married a sister of the said Lemuel Shipp. The will of James Garnett was proved in Woodford County Court in 1808. The children of James and Ann (Shipp) Garnett were: Lewis, Thomas, Anderson, Anthony, Fanny, Elizabeth and Lucy Shipp.

5 Lucy, born about 1759 in Caroline County. She was under age when her father died in 1776/7. She married James Ford and they moved to Woodford County, Kentucky. Their children were: John, Lemuel, Thomas, Susan, Nancy, Lewis, James and Lucy Ford. Richard Doniphan Shipp was executor of the will of James Ford, 1843-1845.

6 Ewell, born about 1763 in Caroline County; in 1776/7 on the death of his father he chose his brother, Gideon Shipp, to be his guardian. In the November, 1788, Caroline Court he brought suit against Richard Pickett. He removed to Kentucky. ( Angelfire says he came to Kentucky in about 1799, but Sanders says that he came with Laban and Colby Shipp, sons of his brother John Shipp, but the parent of Laban and Colby, though named John, was of an earlier generation.)

7 Lemuel Shipp was born in Caroline County circa 1760. He served in the Revolutionary Army as a Privatewith General Nelson’s Corps, Light Dragoons in Baltimore on July 29, 1778. Brother Richard was in the same Corps.. Lemuel Shipp married in King George County by 1783 Lucretia Doniphan, sister of Elizabeth (brother Richard;s wife) daughter of Anderson Doniphan, Gentleman, and Magdalin Monteith, his wife. Lemuel Shipp died in Caroline County and his will was admitted to probate before the June 1788 Court with Thomas Slaughter as executor. After the death of his wife he bequeathed four negroes to;’my brother Richard Shipp;s four daughters namely Mary Shipp, Betsey D. Shipp, Narcissa Shipp and Sophia Shipp.’ According to Sanders, Lemuel and Lucy had 4 children: Richard Jr. who had 10 slaves, Mary, Narcissa and Sophia. If this is correct, one wonders why they weren’t named in his will, although these names bear a striking resemblance to the daughters of his brother Richard who were named in his will. Lucy (Doniphan) Shipp later married the executor, Thomas Slaughter , and she died circa 1804.

There arose concerning the property bequeathed the residuary legatees by Lemuel Shipp a suit in chancery most of which has been published from the original papers filed with the Caroline County Chancery Causes in the Archives Division of the Virginia State Library. It is shown that Thomas Slaughter, the executor of Lemuel Shipp, shortly after his death married his widow Lucy (Doniphan) Shipp, He was then a widower with children of marriageable age, and it would seem absorbed considerable of the Shipp estate.
8 Polly (Martha) As she was under age when her father died in 1776/7, Polly chose James Garnett as her Guardian.
Fanny (Frances). She was born in Caroline Co., married twice (Thomas Sullenter with whom she moved to Woodford Co., KY, he died in 1795; and secondly in 1798 to George Turpin).

John was born in Caroline Co. about 1770 (angelfire) in Caroline Co. (Sanders). Originally, John’s oldest brother Richard Shipp was named as his Guardian, but Richard removed to Kentucky in 1781, and John chose his brother Lemuel as his Guardian. With the death of Lemuel in 1788, John chose a third Guardian, Thomas Garnett. Mr. Garnett sued Thomas Slaughter, executor of Lemuel Shipp for 80 pounds, 10 shillings, for a Bond which Lemuel had held for young John. Thomas Slaughter appeared to be ‘in for the prize’. Young John married on July 2, 1790 in Caroline Co., VA to Lucy Farish, and by 1799 he was about to ‘remove to Kentucky’. He was barely 20, when married, so gained his fourth guardian! (Note: Sanders says he married ..lly Johnson, and had issue, first child being Richard Wyatt Shipp, born April 26, 1750. This would put John as born in approx. 1725, and therefore not one of Thomas and Rachel’s children. Sanders has him attached to the wrong parent.
The following is from Registration in the National Register of Historic Places, 1996 https://npgallery.nps.gov/GetAsset/25e5b8da-ddaa-4498-a146-ea90ce7adb2e:

The property is the 168 acre Sunny Slope, aka the Shipp Farm, a diversified farm established in central Woodford County in 1791 and currently owned and operated by the sixth generation of Shipps. The property contains nineteen historic resources within a diversified agricultural landscape with land use patterns that reflect 19th and 20th century agricultural activities. Included are 16 contributing buildings, one contributing structure and two contributing sites. 1. Main residence, c. 1820, contributing building. The main residence is a one-and-one-half story, rectangular brick masonry, center-passage dwelling built circa 1820 by cabinetmaker/carpenters Richard D and John G. Shipp, sons of the original settler. The main house is listed on the National Register.

Shipp cemetery, c.1830, contributing site. The Shipp family cemetery enclosed with a wire fence containing the marked graves of Richard D. and John C. Shipp the builders of the residence and Sarah Shipp among others not legible

Sunny Slope and nearby Canewood were both built by brothers Richard D. and John G. Shipp, the sons of settlers from Caroline County, Virginia The Shipps built the house at Sunny Slope in 1820 near the site of their parent's cabin of c. 1792 (no longer extant). The one-and-one-half story, center passage home features an elaborate entry with fan and side lights topped by a pedimented portico with Palladian window. Interior details include elaborate mantles with paired colonettes, reeding and breakfront entablatures; door and window frames with corner rosette blocks and fluted trim, and reeded panels beneath windows.
In early 20th century the Shipps were dealers in tobacco seed, and also bred race horses.

It isn’t known if Sunny Slope is still a National Historic Site, and can be visited as such. According to the April 17, 2008 edition of Versailles KY newspaper, The Woodford Sun, the 168 acre Sunny Slope Farm located at 1870 Aiken Road sold April 8 for $3.1 million. The Shipp Family had owned the farm for 6 generations. A little historical background on the farm, reveals that all the way back in the 1780s, Richard and Elizabeth Shipp acquired the place that was then known as The Old Fort Place. Throughout its 200 year history, this Woodford County KY farm has been utilized for everything from growing of hemp, horse farms breeding, raising of cattle, tobacco farming, and even as a dairy farm.
Shipps living in the area in 1996 were:
Early Colonial Settlers of Southern Maryland and Virginia’s Northern Neck Counties. Online at https://www.colonial-settlers-md-va.us/getperson.php?personalID=1028819&tree=tree1
Shipp history from Josiah Shipp mid 1600’s to Rappahannock Co, VA in Genealogies of Virginia Families by Tylers Quarterly and Historical and Genealogical

Shipp Family History found in well documented record: The Shipp Family Genealogy by William Ray Sanders, a descendent. 1946 (see files under Somerville, Corry or William B.) https://archive.org/details/shippgenealogyfr00sand/page/n7/mode/2up
Further Research, possible siblings of Ewell Shipp:
The Children of Thomas and Rachel Shipp were:

1. Richard Shipp is styled in the records Richard Shipp, Senior, to distinguish him from his first cousin of the same name who is styled Richard Shipp, Junior. Richard Shipp, eldest child of Thomas and Rachel Shipp, was born in Caroline County, Virginia, 12th of November, 1747; of him more subsequently.

2. Gideon Shipp was born in Caroline County circa 1750. He resided in Essex County, where he married Mrs. Alice (Dunn), Emmerson, daughter of William Dunn, and widow of James Emmerson, of Essex. On 2 July 1790 Gideon Shipp, in a very courtly hand, penned a letter to Captain James Edmondson praying he would stop the sale of the said Shipp's personal property to satisfy a certain judgement. Gideon Shipp died in Essex County prior to 14 June 1797, when his four children, Alice, Katy, Thomas and Ann Shipp, had legal guardians appointed.

3. Edmund Shipp was born in Caroline County in 1753. He states in the preamble of his will, dated 5 January 1816 and proved in Jefferson County, Kentucky, 11 March 1816, he is aged sixty-three years. He married Tibitha Garnett, who survived him. His children maned in his will were: Nancy Shipp, Sally G. Jowell, Betsey Shipp, Luch Shipp, Thomas Shipp, Edmund Shipp (died unmarried, 1823), and Ewell Shipp. Edmund Shipp owned 445 acres of land in Caroline County, which he sold before moving to Kentucky in 1794.

4. Ann Shipp, born in Caroline County circa 1755, married James Garnett; they moved to Woodford County, Kentucky. In a deposition made in Woodford County 6 October 1806 James Garnett deposes in a suit relative to the estate of Lemuel Shipp of Caroline County, deceased, in which he states that he was well acquainted with the "very handsome personal estate possessed by Lemuel Shipp, having married a sister of the said Lemuel Shipp." The will of James Garnett was proved in Woodford County Court in 1808. the children of James and Ann (Shipp) Garnett were: Lewis, Thomas, Anderson, Anthony, Fanny, Elizabeth and Lucy Shipp.

5. Lucy Shipp was born in Caroline County circa 1757. She was yet under age when her father died in 1777. She married James Ford and they moved to Woodford County, Kentucky. Their children were: John, Lemuel, Thomas, Susan, Nancy, Lewis, James and Lucy Ford. Richard Domiphan Shipp was executor of the will of James Ford, 1843-1845.

6. Lemuel Shipp was born in Caroline County circa 1760. He served in the Revolutionary Army with General Nelson's Corps, Light Dragoons. Lemuel Shipp married in King George County by 1783 Lucretia ("Lucy") Doniphan, daughter of Anderson Doniphan, Gentleman, and Magdalin Nonteith, his wife. Lemuel Shipp died without issue in Caroline County and his will was admitted to probate before the June 1788 Court with Thomas Slaughter as executor. A full copy of his will has been published, which was dated 13 April 1787. After the death of his wife he bequeathed four negroes to "my brother Richard Ship's four daughters namely Mary Ship, Betsey D. Ship, Narcissa Ship and Sopha Ship" and to his will appointed his wife executrix and Mr. Honathan Finnall executor. Mrs Lucy (Doniphan) Shipp Slaughter died circa 1804.

There arose concerning the property bequeathed the residuary legatees by Lemuel Shipp a suit in chancery most of which has been published from the original papers filed with the Caroline County Chancery Causes in the Archives Division of the Virginia State Library. It is shown that Thomas Slaughter, the executor of Lemuel Shipp, shortly after his death married his widow Lucy (Doniphan) Shipp, He was then a widower with children of marriageable age, and it would seem absorbed considerable of the Shipp estate.

Filed with these chancery papers is the deposition of Mr. Anderson Doniphan, of Stafford County, aged about 25 years, taken 1 September 1789 in which he says that in 1787 Mr. Richard Shipp came to the County of King George and informed the deponent the sheriff of Caroline had distrained a desk the property of Lemuel Shipp, deceased, and that he the said Shipp had come over to get the taxes from Mrs. Shipp, the relict of the aforesaid Lemuel Shipp . . . and after the aforesaid conversation the deponent went in company with the said Richard Shipp to Mr. Finnalls in Stafford County, where Mrs. Shipp had gone and the deponent saw Mrs. Shipp, later Mrs. Slaughter, pay the said Shipp a piece of gold. The deponent, Anderson Domiphan, was a first cousin of Mrs. Lemuel Shipp, who after the death of her husband seems to have gone on an extended visit to her step-father and mother, Mr. and Mrs Jonathan Finnall, in Stafford County Virginia.

7. Ewell Shipp was born in Caroline County; in 1777 on the death of his father he chose his brother, Gideon Shipp, to be his guardian. In the November, 1788, Caroline Court he brought suit against Richard Pickett. He is said to have removed to Kentucky.
8. Martha (?Molly) Shipp. Chose James Garnett her guardian after death of her father.

9. Frances (Fanny) Shipp was born in Caroline County. She married first Thomas Sullenter and with him moved to Woodford County, Kentucky, where he died in 1795. She married secondly, in 1798 George Turpin.

10. John Shipp-, seemingly the youngest of the children of Thomas and Rachel Shipp, was born in Caroline County circa 1770. In a deposition in Shelby County, Kentucky, in 1806 Richard Shipp says that he was guardian for his younger brother John and after some years the said John chose Lemuel Shipp, deceased, to be his guardian, and after the death of Lemuel Shipp "John Ship choose a third guardian, Thomas Garnett." As guardian to John Shipp, Lemuel Shipp held a bond for #87:10:0, which passed to Thomas Slaughter, the executor of Lemuel Shipp. In November 1788, "Thomas Garnett, guardian of John Ship," brought suit against "Thomas Slaughter, administrator of Lemuel Ship, deceased." John Shipp married in Caroline County on 2 July 1790 Lucy Farish. By 1799 he is stated to have been residing in either Frederick or Berkley County, Va., and "about to remove to Kentucky."

In a letter from Corry to his brother Tenison in July 1857, Corry describes Eliza as “a Bellingham - black eyes and black hair, fair skin considered pretty, married to John Gamble, a red hot Orangeman from the black north, a good farmer.”

Like all her sisters, except Dorothea, Eliza married in her mid teens, as she was barely 15 when she married John Gamble in Thorold, ON, and honeymooned in Niagara Falls, Ontario, just a few miles away. The first 9 of their 14 children were born in Thorold, Ontario, with the first being James, born October 14, 1850. It is possible that baby James was born at the home of John’s parents in London Township, Canada (according to Gamble family historian, George Hart), but this is uncertain, as John and Eliza Gamble were living next to her parents in Caistor, Lincoln Twp in 1851 with their 2 year old son, James.

Immigration records show that John and Eliza Gamble and their family moved to Cleveland in 1867, where John was a brickmaker. Their next 5 children were born in Cleveland. Eliza was having children at the same time as her oldest son, James Mitchell Gamble. James started his family in Cleveland, where he was a brickmaker, then, with his large family, moved to Los Angeles between 1883 and 1887 and established a large brickmaking enterprise. While Eliza and John died and are burried in Ellsworth, Pierce, Wisconsin, most of their children moved to Los Angeles area.

Hugh Stevenson married Eliza's sister Dorothea Somerville in Cleveland. It is possible that he went there because of his good friend and London neighbour, John Gamble. Hugh became a brickmaker, like John Gamble and his brother James Gamble, who also had emigrated to Cleveland in about 1864.
Census 1851, living in Caistor Township, Ontario
Census June 1, 1870 living in Cleveland, OH
Census June 10, 1880 living in Pierce, Wisc
Source: Somerville Index and Wendy Stevenson

Maggie and Sinicoe birthed their first 4 children in Welland County, Ontario, Canada. They removed to Cleveland in 1869 with her parents, Corry and Lucinda Somerville, as well as her sister Eliza Gamble, and her husband John. In 1870 Maggie and Sinicoe and their children were living with Corry and Lucinda in a hotel at 911 Broadway St., in Cleveland, located where Jacob’s Field is now. Corry was ‘keeping the hotel’. Also living in the hotel were Maggie’s newlywed sister Dorothea and her husband Hugh Stevenson.

Maggie had a close relationship with sister Dorothea, and they kept up regular correspondence after Dorothea and Hugh returned to Bosanquet Township in Canada in about 1877. They also visited each other quite regularly, making the long train ride, or taking the boat train across Lake Erie from Cleveland to Port Stanley, then by rail to Thedford, Bosanquet Township.

Maggie appeared to have been a kind-hearted soul. With the early deaths of 2 of her younger sisters, Henrietta and Lucinda, Maggie took on the role of parenting their orphaned children. By 1880 Mysie Street (daughter of Henrietta, deceased) was living with Maggie and Sinicoe, even though Mysie’s father was still living. In addition, Nelson McKinnon, son of sister Lucinda, deceased was also living with Maggie. Lucinda’s other children, Ida and Mysie McKinnon were living with her sister, Dorothea Stevenson, in Canada. Sadly Nelson died just two years later, at about age 10, from ‘exhaustion’, meaning tuberculosis.
Notes: Margaret Adelaide and Simcoe had 5 children.
Source: Somerville Index and Wendy Stevenson..

paras: 3rd daughter of Corry Somerville (0586) and Lucinda Simonton (0587).
Baptised March 1, 1844, St. Paul’s Episcopal Church, Rochester, New York
Marriage: 24 January 1870, Hugh Stevenson (0621) son of Robert Stevenson and
Elizabeth Connaghty Stevenson, in Cleveland, Ohio.
Death: 16 September 1922, Jericho, Bosanquet Twp, Lambton Co, Ontario

In a letter written to his brother Tenison, in July 1867, Corry described his daughter Dorothea as “black hair, black eyes and skin of the same colour, considered very clever and very handsome. I will say very good - hard work to keep her from being taken away. [The height, black hair and dark eyes have been passed on through the generations, as her descendants are very tall, dark haired, although some have green eyes like Dorothea's husband, Hugh, who was a "stubborn red-headed Irishman"!]

Dorothea’s early education was either in Rochester, NY or Caistor Township, Ontario. She had probably met her future husband while the family was living in Caistor, as her sister, Eliza, had married Hugh Stevenson’s close friend, John Gamble. Dorothea moved with her parents to Buffalo, New York, area before settling in Cleveland, Ohio.

Dorothea didn`t marry Hugh Stevenson until she was 30, and after the family had migrated to Cleveland, in January 1870. Hugh had previously purchased a farm at Lot 11, Concession 8, Bosanquet Twp, Ontario on November 15, 1866, but he didn’t stay there for very long, as he had moved to Cleveland by January 1870, when he married Dorothea Somerville. Their first 3 children were born in Cleveland, Somerville Bellingham Stevenson, Thomas McIlroy, Stevenson, Rosay and her twin, Quayle, who died in infancy. By February 1880, the family had returned to the4 farm in Canada, where Robert Corry was born. The family continued to reside at ‘the home place’, where both Hugh and Dorothea died, and Robert Corry lived at the farm until just before his death. The home was originally a one story log building, which met the Settlement Duty of the original patent owners, but Hugh added a second storey and a back porch to accommodate his growing family. For part of the time, two of Dorothea’s nieces from her deceased sisters Henrietta (Mysie Street) and Lucinda (Ida MacKinnon) lived with the family at the farm.

Dorothea was known as Aunt Dolly to many. She raised her nieces Ida McKinnon (from sister Lucinda Kate), and Mysie Street (from sister Alicia) with her own children. She must have been a prolific writer, as we have copies of over 250 post cards in 2 year period. It was clearly important for her to keep in touch with her family, especially those in Cleveland, with whom she was particularly close.

Dorothea and Hugh continued to live in ‘the home farm’, after her son Robert Corry was married to Katherine and raising their own children there. Dorothea’s granddaughter, Florence Stevenson, had fond memories of her Grandmother Dorothea, as shown in this excerpt:

“My father, Robert Corry Stevenson, was the youngest child of Grampa Hugh and Grandma Dorothea Victoria. Grandma Dorothea was a very talented, artistic person. She played the violin, the grand piano, and loved to dance. She taught my father to dance and he was known in the community for his excellence. I, personally, would agree, since he was the best partner I ever danced with. The ballroom was on the second floor of the general store in the village of Thedford, between four and five miles from the farm. The story goes that my father would walk down the railroad track to the village and the same home. He had a full length Beaver coat which he wore – put his dancing shoes in the pockets, and off to the Ball. The story goes that Grandma never slept soundly until “Robbie was home. She had bricks warming in the oven to put in his bed when he arrived home and didn’t worry about time when he wakened in the morning.
Grandma, or “Aunt Doll” as she was known in the community, was reported to make the ‘best’ pickles on the 8th Concession.

My brother, Don, had blonde curly hair until he was about three years old. Father couldn’t abide that ‘his son’ had curls so he proceeded to cut his hair one afternoon. Grandma Dorothea lived with us on the farm. She was so indignant that the ‘baby’s’ curls were cut off that she packed her satchel and walked the half mile up to Aunt Rosie Catt’s, until she calmed down.”

The 1920 US census shows Grandma Dolly as visiting nephew Serle Dennis in Cleveland, where she had made the long journey, transferring trains, at the age of 80. She died at home on the farm just two years later.
1 Somerville Bellingham Stevenson, b.20 July 1871, married, and had issue d.July 1918, Bozeman,
Montana, where he had been a teamster, and after a fight at a saloon, where he was defending a woman’s honour.
2 Thomas McIlroy Stevenson , b.27 November 1873, Cleveland, Ohio, married and had issue d. 1944
Arkona, Ontario. Uncle Tim, as he was known, was a telegraph operator, and spent many years living in New Mexico, before returning to Canada.
3 Rose Eliza, twin, b. 11 April 1875 Cleveland Ohio, married and had issue. After her marriage, Rosie lived just a couple of farms over from her parents.d.18 February 1954,Jericho..
4 Quayle Stevenson,twin, b. 11 April 1875 d.24 July 1875-cholera.Cleveland, Ohio
5 Robert Corry Stevenson, b.14 February 1880, Jericho, md. Katherine McLeod
17 March 1915 in Thedford, Lambton Co, Ontario and had 4 children: Florence (Lawrence Lindeman),

Margaret (Morley Gough), Donald Somerville Stevenson (Marjorie Bannister) – father of Wendy Stevenson’s husband, Robert (Bob) Stevenson,- and Robert Gordon Stevenson (Peggy Clay). Robert Corry Stevenson was a tax collector and farmer, and remained at the home farm until just before his death.

Notes: Hugh emigrated to Canada in 1854 with his parents and siblings from Grace Hill Moravian community in Ahoghil, Co Antrim.
Hugh was the youngest child of Robert Stevenson and his wife Elizabeth Connaghty Stevenson. Their issue were:
John Stevenson, born Ireland, May 19, 1824 (d London, ON, 1895), married Sophia McLeod
Samuel, born Ireland May 2, 1827 (died London, ON 1893), married Mary Keown
Sarah Jane, born Ireland Sept 13, 1829 (died London ON 1916), married in Ireland to Robert Clare
Eliza Margaret, born Ireland May 4, 1832, died in canada
Mary, born January 24, 1834 in Ireland (d. Bosanquet Twp., Ontario 1915), married Hugh Clark
Nancy, born Ireland Febrary 7 1837 (d Bosanquet Twp., Ontario 1921), married David Sloan
Rosa, born Ireland October 22, 1839 (d. London, ON 1921), married Sam Sloan
Hugh, born Ireland, March 1842 (d. Bosanquet Twp. Ontario 1915), married Dorothea Somerville

Robert was the last of five brothers, sons of John Stevenson and Mary Rankin Stevenson to leave Ireland. Between 1845 and 1849 a severe potato blight had affected the potato crops in Ireland with disastrous effects for the population. It is known as The Great Famine. Times were hard for Protestants, politically, socially, and economically, but they were much harder for the Catholics, who had few voting rights, and no land ownership. Robert and Elizabeth and their eight children were not as badly off as many, but dreams of better lives were dominant in their Moravian Community. Their oldest sons John and Samuel left home in 1848, and we know from his obituary that Sam lived for a year in Lower Canada, possibly with Uncle Philip. Robert emigrated 1852. Sam saved enough (hopefully with contributions from his father!) to return to Ireland in order to bring back his mother Elizabeth, his younger sisters and Hugh, in 1854. Sister Sarah Jane remained behind in Ahoghill with her husband Robert Clare and their older children, but they also came to Canada in 1857, staying on a second small home on the property with her parents, Robert and Elizabeth. Sam met Mary Keown on the boat back to Canada, and they married in 1856, returned to London, and he became a brickmaker in Westminster Township for seven years.

The journey to the new land took about six weeks, and was made on an open sail boat. Many immigrants at that time, mainly from Ireland, died on or after the journey as a result of cholera or other disease. The Stevenson family bible from 1772 survived the journey in their pine trunk, but suffered salt water damage. The family brought seed potatoes for their new life, but apparently needed to eat them en route. They also brought cock-fighting regalia. Family lore says that Hugh had stowed away on the trip to Canada, to save money on fares!

To encourage settlement, the Crown gave any British Citizen land, free of charge, if he or she fulfilled certain settlement duties: the settler was obliged to clear five acres of land for each 100 he wished to claim, open a road in front of his lot, and build a log house of at least 16 feet by 20 feet, and occupy it! If these stipulations were completed within 18 months, the Crown issued a patent to the settler, indicating that the ownership of the land had passed from the Crown to the individual.

Many settlers were well established in their places of origin, but came to Upper Canada to improve the prospects of their families or to escape deteriorating social and economic conditions. Settlers often travelled in family groups and came out to join relatives already in Upper Canada. Brothers William and Robert migrated from Gracehill, Ahoghill as part of a group of seven families who all settled in the Crumlin area: Stevenson, Sloan, Clark, Clare, Kernohan, Gamble and Russell. The families intermarried. John Gamble and Hugh Stevenson seem to have been life-long friends, as they both married Somerville sisters, John to Eliza in Thorold and Hugh to Dorothea in Cleveland. John returned to London for awhile as his first child was born there, but he migrated to Cleveland where Hugh later joined him at the end of 1869.

In 1861 Hugh was living in London with his parents and sister Rosanna. He was listed as absent from home. His parents` home was next door to Robert Clare and Hugh's sister Sarah Stevenson Clare, who had immigrated in 1857 according to census report. By November 1866, Hugh had purchased a farm at Lot 11, Concession 8, Bosanquet Twp, but he didn’t live there for very long, as he had moved to Cleveland by January 1870, when he married Dorothea Somerville.

Aunt Dollie, granddaughter of Hugh and Dorothea says of Hugh: "He could have been very prosperous but he was sort of a rover, and he liked cockfights. I don't know what took him to Cleveland, I guess just drifting about. He was a policeman in Cleveland and voted there and he never was a citizen, they was not so fussy then. Granny fell in love with him because he was so handsome. He was red haired and had long red whiskers. I sat on his lap and braided and combed his hair and whiskers when I was wee and he liked that. Granny was educated and refined and very intelligent. Granny was a pianist and elocutionist. She gave me the blackthorn cane and granddad's grog jug because I was the only daughter of the eldest son. The names Corry and McElroy as I remember are family friends. One of them was the name of a beau of Grannys before she fell in love with Granddad. She was 29 when she married and granddad was about 1-1/2 years younger and everyone twitted her about marrying such an old man.”

The first four children of Hugh and Dorothea were born in Cleveland: Somerville Bellingham Stevenson, Thomas McIlroy, Stevenson, Rosay and her twin, Quayle, who died as an infant. Hugh and Dorothea and their oldest children returned to the farm in Canada in 1877, where Robert Corry was born in 1880. The family continued to reside at ‘the home place’, where both Hugh and Dorothea died, and Robert Corry lived at the farm until just before his death in 1965.

The home was originally a one story log building, which met the Settlement Duty of the original patent owners, but Hugh added a second storey and a back porch to accommodate his growing family, and also built a large barn. For part of the time, two of Dorothea’s nieces from her deceased sisters Henrietta (Mysie Street) and Lucinda (Ida MacKinnon) lived with the family at the farm. At one time he attempted to operate a brickyard, with his brother John, on the farm opposite him on the 8th Concession. Apparently most of the brick homes in that area were made from Stevenson brick, but the business eventually failed as the farm did not yield enough clay to make the bricks. Several Gamble and Stevenson men were brickmakers, and apparently John Gamble and Hugh Stevenson had arms ‘like tree trunks’ as a result of their work at their brickyard in Cleveland.

Degree of the Loyal Orange Lodge, No 230 is granted to Brother Hugh Stevenson on 18th day of July, 18?? And signed by [his brother in law] Deputy Master Robert Clare. Ahoghill Loyal Orange Lodge #230 was originally founded in 1838 with a new warrant being issued to North Dorchester, Ontario area in April, 1848. The lodge was moved to Crumlin (now a part of London, Ontario) on February 23, 1850 and was named Ahoghill after the Irish home-town of some of the founders. The lodge initially met in a brick lodge room erected just east of Crumlin; near the Stevenson farms.
Source: Somerville Index and Wendy Stevenson.

BAS’ life is best considered in three parts; the early years up to his marriage in 1879, the middle years up to his retirement in 1891 and the ‘Clermont’ years from 1891 until his early death in 1916.

Little is recorded about BAS’ childhood except that, unlike his children, he was sent to school in Dublin where he was born in 1853; it has been suggested that he was assertive or precocious and was known as ‘Fighting Attie’. He was the fourth of five brothers born to Tenison Alan Somerville (0591), who, following his return from Trinidad in 1846, had secured a position as a public servant in the secretariat of the RIC in Dublin Castle. His eldest brother, William Denniston Somerville, who was born in Trinidad in 1842, was dumb following a disastrous operation in early childhood and lived quietly with his parents and subsequently with BAS and his wife; his second brother, Tenison Alan Somerville, also born in Trinidad in 1845, died at the age of ten in 1855 after the family had come back to Ireland; his third brother, Henry Bellingham Somerville born in Dublin in 1848, was a District Inspector in the RIC; his youngest brother, also called Tenison Alan Somerville (Sonnie), born four

years after his namesake’s death in 1859, seemed to have suffered throughout his life from some unrecorded psychological impediment and, although able to live a relatively normal life, was at all times in the care of his parents, his brothers Henry or BAS and, after his parents’ death, his sister, Erina (Cis/Amy)
and her husband The Rev. Thomas Rolfe, in Yorkshire. Amy was born in Dublin in 1851.

BAS started a personal diary on 9 July 1869, when he was 15 years old, which, however, was written up subsequently from letters and memoranda. This shows enjoyable teenage years; from July to December 1869, he was with Henry who was stationed at Claremorris in the west of Ireland, walking and mountaineering, fishing and shooting, hunting, with Henry’s men, for ‘poteen’, ‘stills’ and ‘worms’ and making large s

zures, visiting archeological sites, and staying with various friends. This was the pattern for two or three years. At home, initially, 48, Gloucester Street in the City and subsequently, Prospect House, Ranelagh, there was much entertainment and dancing. BAS was already showing an interest in history; the entry for 21 September 1870 reads “When in Trinity College this day, I saw the skeleton of John Temple, Provost of the College in 1609. He was buried in 1689 but where was unknown till this day when some workmen digging up the ground under the central tower in the College (the Campanile) came upon the coffin. I believe that the late Palmerston some years ago made a very strong effort to find out where John Temple, his ancestor, was buried but could not succeed.”

had already started his family research; the entry for 16 December 1870 reads as follows: “Father’s birthday. I finished this day the first genealogical tree I ever made of our family and gave it to P. It is six feet five inches long by eighteen inches broad and has taken me from 28 April to make, seven months and two days”. 1871 continued in the same vein;1 June – a dance at Prospect, 17 June – Civil Service Sports at Exhibition Gardens, I ran 3rd in 100 yards race, Sonnie got 2nd in the boys’ race. Had dance at Prospect, Josie Armstrong and the two Miss Williamsons staying here, 20 October – had a letter from Sir Alan Bellingham enclosing an introduction to the Library of the Royal Dublin Society, 27 November - I went in the evening to the opening of the Gaiety Theatre, Mrs Scott Siddons read the address; the play was ‘She Stoops to Conquer’ followed by ‘La Belle Sauvage’

1872 sees BAS’ first contact with the RIC. On 20 April he receives a nomination for cadetship; there were two vacancies, eight candidates, so he began to work hard with the Tutor, Mr Crawley. On 7 May he was medically examined and had an oral with the Inspector General, Col Sir John Stewart-Wood. 28 to 30 May, he sat the exams.

The entry for 16 June “I got a letter from the Civil Service Commissioners in London saying that I had got first place at the examination. All were very glad. Poor Mother cried over it” 11 July 1872 – “I joined the RI Constabulary Depot

On 19 July 1872 BAS was issued his Journal at the Phoenix Park Depot and started life as a Cadet; the journal remained with him throughout his career and was entered up daily until sickness forced him to leave office on 3 August 1890. After ceaseless parading, drilling and orderly duties at the Depot, he was posted to take charge of the Charleville district in north west Cork on 1 February 1873. District duties included parading and drilling, ball firing, inspecting sub Barracks at sub districts all over north Cork and east Limerick –Milford, Buttevant, Liscarrol, Churchtown, Kilmallock and Freemount – attending Assizes and Petty Sessions, investigating outrages, arresting and prosecuting felons, dealing with insubordination of the men, paying staff and pensioners, attending, with mobile patrols, disturbances within and without the District etc. Times were disturbed and getting worse with the Fenian troubles being followed by Land League intimidation and seizures and wounding of stock, non payment of rents and subsequent evictions. But BAS also had a social life; he was constantly visiting , either on short leave or ‘private business’ places such as Limerick, Cork, Rathkeale, Mallow, Kilfinnane, Newcastle, Youghal and Dublin. When he left the District on transfer to Newtownhamilton in Co Armagh on 1 March 1876, owing to the amalgamation of Charleville with Mallow and Kanturk, his private diary records – “ I have served three years at Charleville and during that time enjoyed myself but ran heavily into debt. I found all the people very kind to me and attended all the gay doings in Cork and Limerick and on the borders of Tipperary and Waterford during that time. The following families were very hospitable and kind to me and many a pleasant day I spent at their places. Sanders of Sanders Park, Harrisons of Castle Harrison ( his eldest son Bunt was to marry General Harrison’s eldest daughter Kitty 50 years later), Hutchins of Fortlands, Barrys of Kilbolane Castle, Drews of Drewscourt, Sheltons of Rossmore, Weldons of Cooline, Bruces of Miltown Castle, Sullivans of Curramore, Weldons of Highfort, Barrys of Ballyvonaise, Moore- Smyths of Ballynatray, Creaghs of Creagh Castle, Franks of Carrig Park, Wilkinsons of St Oswalds, Finches of Maryville, The O’Gradys of Athlacca. The 1st Battalion of 20th Regt under Col Davies and afterwards a Battalion of 25th Regt under Col Ruddell were at Buttevant nine miles from Charleville and I spent a great portion of my time with them”. While at Charleville and throughout his career, BAS kept buying and selling horses; whether for personal or professional use, is not clear. Clearly, however, he was having an enjoyable time, and, no doubt, living above his means.

While the duties at NewtownHamilton were, in theory, much the same, they were more intense; there seemed to be more numerous and more serious disturbances. The District included Keady, Cullyhanna, Crossmaglen, Silverbridge and Carnagh. But there was still time to make visits on private business to Portadown, Armagh, Newry and Castleblayney. BAS, however, seemed to have a ‘flying’ squad of men and he was detailed to attend Orange disturbances and open riots outside his district, particularly in Belfast .

On 1 March 1878, he was ordered to proceed to the Phoenix Park Depot and to report to Dublin Castle the following day. The reason is not clear, but there follows a period of five and a half months’ parading and drilling, as if he had been in some trouble; indeed, on 30 April 1878, he was suspended from duty and pay until the following 1 July when he was reinstated in rank and pay. On 13 August, he resumed command of Newtownhamilton. Even during his period at the Depot, he was put in command of a ‘flying’ squad of 20 men from the Co Carlow force to attend the Orange anniversary on 12 July at Gilford, Co Down.

During his time at NewtownHamilton, BAS started suffering from recurring bouts of neuralgia and headaches and put himself on sick leave; he also sprained his ankle early on in his career, and he had continuing trouble with it, so much so that he was dragged down by it constantly until he was forced to retire. The bright part of his stay in Co Armagh, were his visits to Witney and his engagement to Margaret Hall Clinch in January/February 1878.

On 1 April 1879, BAS was transferred at his own request to Newtownards, Co Down. This was a large and important urban centre, with substantial, populous sub districts and barracks at Comber, Kircubbin, Holywood, Bangor, Killinchy, NewtownBreda, Donaghadee, Greyabbey and Portaferry. With his greater responsibilities and marriage to Margaret Hall Clinch on 27 August 1879, social activities seem to figure less prominently; rather, the duties of the larger district seem more widespread and onerous. The disturbances caused by the activities of the Land League, now the National League, and the potential for disturbance caused by elections and the ceremonies of the Orange Order, see BAS in action with a ‘flying’ squad in such distant places as Coleraine, Trim, Dungannon and Belfast. He spends January and February 1881 at Hollymount in Co Mayo where a new District is formed and where on 22 January, he is protecting John Lynskey, bailiff to Capt Boycott near Balla, with 50 men and a company of the 76th Regiment in expectation of trouble from the Land League at evictions. Back in Newtownards, he is protecting Lord Annesley for two months, until his lordship finally departs Ireland; and constantly patrolling Clandeboye. The entry for 7 May 1882 reads:” At office. Received telegram stating that Lord Frederick Cavendish (the Chief Secretary) and J H Burke (the Under Secretary) had been murdered in the Phoenix Park at 7.15 pm last night. Telegraphed to all the outstations; had suspects looked up and the trains and cars watched. On patrol from 6.00pm to 8.00 pm and from 10.00pm till 1.00am.”

By 1883, he is seeking a transfer; on 1 May he is transferred at his own request to Queenstown, Co Cork. This again is a substantial and populous district, with the added responsibility of supervising visiting trans Atlantic ships, which feature frequently in the journal. Criminals wanted in America are seized and those suspected of fomenting trouble in Ireland are investigated. The sub districts include Glanmire, Passage, Spike Island (a holding base for prisoners whch involves escorted transfers to Mountjoy in Dublin), Haulbowline, Monkstown, Crosshaven and others. BAS is still involved with a ‘flying’ squad; in July 1886, he goes the whole way up to Downpatrick in Co Down on special duty. He still suffers from a sore foot.
The journal for 8 March 1887 and the following days reads as follows:

“At office. Inspected Crosshaven at 10.15 am, Passage West from 11.30 am till 12.00. Proceeded by 5.00 pm train to Youghal (on the border of Co Cork and Co Waterford) on ? duty. On march from Railway Station to the Barracks, we were ferociously attacked and I charged the mob three times when they were dispersed. One man Patrick Hanlon died from a sword stab inflicted in the charge”
“On duty in Youghal. A verdict of culpable murder preferred by Coroner’s jury against Const. Ward and myself.”
“I was arrested by D I Kerin of Youghal and lodged in the County jail with Const Ward.”
“In County jail. By Order of the Queens Bench, I was released this day on bail myself in £500. Const Ward also released on his own bail £50.”
“Returned to Queenstown at 1.30 am but did not resume duty.”
“A Nolle Prosequi having been entered by the Attorney General at Assizes in case of murder against Const Ward and myself, I resumed duty this day. Attended at Divisional Magistrate’s Office on duty.”

For the next few months, BAS carried on his normal duties, but there were frequent meetings with superiors on confidential business, other District Inspectors, County Inspectors and Divisional Magistrates. One can imagine that it would have been difficult for BAS to continue as DI in Queenstown, so near to Youghal.

On 1 December 1887, BAS is transferred at his own request to Wicklow. The district is far flung; it embraces Wicklow, Redcross, Rathdrum, Avoca, Arklow, Rathnew and Ashford and elsewhere. The duties are much the same as in previous districts, although he is frequently called to protect Protestants at open air religious meetings in Arklow, but the journal shows that after the initial two years, his heart doesn’t seem to be in it. He suffers increasingly from his sore foot, lameness, sore throat and swollen face and unspecified sickness; and takes numerous single days leave. For instance, in January 1889, he is out sick for 6 successive days, then in the office for 1 day, then on 1 day’s leave, followed by 6 successive days sickness, 1 days leave and 2 days absence with a lame foot. Similar patterns of sickness emerge for the next two months; in March he describes himself on three occasions as being ‘very ill’. In April 1889, he is sick all month and again between 1 and 16 May. He then goes on leave between 17 May and 2 June, resuming duty on 3 June 1889. By the summer of 1890, he is sick again and the journal finally ends on 2 August 1890 when he stays at home sick. In effect, BAS ceases duties in 1890 although the belief is that he formally retired in the following year.

There seems to have been something of a shadow over BAS’ career; he was obviously a popular officer; perhaps unambitious; with several unexplained hiccups in the initial years. He held good appointments in NewtownHamilton and Newtownards, but why was there no promotion to County Inspector? Was his candidature for promotion the reason for the five month session at the Depot in 1878? He was then still only 25 and, for some unknown reason, he blotted his copy book temporarily while at the Depot. However, after the trouble at Youghal, it would have been politically difficult to secure promotion. One can imagine the howls of protest from the nationalist community and Roman Catholic Church. He seems thereafter to have been dispirited, as one would suspect, and plagued by ill health. It is, perhaps, not surprising that he threw in the towel , even though he was still under 40 years of age.

Regi said that after his retirement BAS wanted to buy Myrtle Grove in Youghal; it is a charming 15th/16th century town house that had belonged to, or, at any rate, occupied by Sir Walter Raleigh and one can still see the attractions. He was advised against it, for obvious reasons. There followed a number of moves; the family rented Friars Hill, in Wicklow Town between 1890 and 1892; it seems they may then have moved to 82, Harcourt Street in Dublin for two years. By 1894, Clermont, at Rathnew, was on the market. It would, undoubtedly, have been known to BAS when stationed in Wicklow. In fact, the Chomley family, who held the Fee Farm Grant of the property since the 1840s had fallen on hard times and the Landed Estate Court had been seeking a buyer since 1879. An auction was directed in 1894 and, although BAS bid for it, the successful bidder was Col C G Tottenham of Ballycurry, Ashford. It is said that he didn’t wish Clermont to fall into undesirable hands. Immediately after the auction, he offered the place to BAS, whom he had known when the latter was in Wicklow, for the price at which he had bought it - £1,800. The property was in appalling condition, so BAS and the family had to continue renting while repairs and alterations were undertaken. They therefore rented Ballyhenry near Ashford from Dr Truell, and, thereafter, Seaview House in Wicklow Town which they had occupied when BAS was first appointed to Wicklow in 1887.

After the purchase, Clermont was fully renovated and plumbed. Two new wings were added. The wing on the northern end was two storey and contained a sewing room , a dark room, a small study and kitchen quarters on the ground floor, three bedrooms, dressing room, bathroom and servants rooms upstairs. The south wing, which was of larger scale and proportions

, so as not to unbalance the appearance of the house, contained a large drawing room, a billiard room, long panelled passage and hall and cloakroom with a door leading to the grounds on the south of the house. The ceiling in the drawing room was elaborately decorated and that in the billiard room had circular windows in the roof and a frieze decorated with the Somerville crest and arms.
Cecil who was 14 years old when BAS bought the property describes the place at that time as follows:

“At one time all the land round and about belonged to the Yarners and the family ultimately ended with three sisters, either daughters or grand daughters of Sir Abraham Yarner. The property was divided into three portions, now (1944 when this was written) represented by Clonmannon, Clermont and Rossanagh, and each girl received one. The girl to whose lot Clonmannon fell married a Truell
(when she was a widow, her name being Catherine Stone, many years older than Holt Truell)

and there have been Truells at Clonmannon ever since. The other two shares, either by marriage or purchase, fell into other hands and in time were divided up. There was an old house at Clermont which stood somewhere about where the present stables are, but that house was burnt down, and the present house has its date over the front door – 1730. (In fact, the old house stood in the south west corner of the yard)

There was a Rev. Francis Chomley, M.A.,who was Rector of Wicklow. He had a son Francis and two daughters, Jane and Lucy. (In fact, he had three daughters). The Chomleys kept up great state at Clermont and the gardens were particularly nice with lavender hedges etc. Francis Chomley was a tea merchant in China, and, after his father’s death, he used to send money to his sisters for the upkeep of the place. After some years, he returned home and was horrified to find that they had neglected everything, and that they had let the house, garden and all, fall into a state of disrepair. He had had bad sunstroke abroad, and the disappointment when he got home quite turned his brain and he set to destroy everything. He broke down a forge, laundry and dairy which were in the yard, and a forge near the village, tore up hedges and cut down many fine trees in front of the house and let in the villagers to collect the wood. He laughed at them fighting over it. According to Matty Doyle (1944) who lived in a pretty cottage at the corner of the Rathnew/Newrath road with Tighes Avenue, there was an entrance to Clermont at the end of the moat field, and the avenue came up through the moat field, sandhill field and Rathnew field, and through a gateway with large gateposts into the wood opposite Clarke’s farm.(This became the ‘Jubilee Avenue’ to mark Queen Victoria’s Jubilee, started by BAS, but not totally finished).

The field on the left hand side of the path going down to the gardens was known as Keogh’s field because a man named Keogh live in a cottage in the N.W. corner of the field which looked onto the lane running along the boundary of Clermont , known as the Bullock Walk. Along the side of the garden, the paths went around a moat which went down the west and south of the garden and was fed by a small stream from the Rathnew river. Inside the garden were many small flower beds enclosed by box hedges, and beyond that a high laurel hedge with three arches and a granite pillar for a sundial in the centre.

After we settled in, my father made many improvements. (Perhaps, all or some were made before they moved in as they continued to rent until 1895 and there was evidently snow on the ground when they moved in) He added two wings to the house, made a large lawn in front, then a terrace at the back, widened the path to the garden, and planted trees and shrubs on each side. He enlarged the moat on the west side into a large pond. Sir Thomas Drew, the architect for the new wings, and Messrs Pemberton, the builders, while doing repairs to the coachman’s house, discovered a cornice. This, it was thought, must have been part of the old house which is said to have stood in the present stableyard and is said to have been burnt down. Sir Thomas very much admired the old belfry in the yard wall near the house. He thought it was Flemish work. In later years, we were told it was one of the last examples of Flemish work in Ireland.(This was taken down by the nuns who ultimately bought the property)

By the large beech trees outside the garden gate, there was a lavender bush when we first came to Clermont. Old Kinsella, who lived at the lodge with his wife, Judy, said this was all that was left of the old lavender hedge of which there used to be so much at Clermont. There is still (1944) an old myrtle tree by the small gate going into the yard from the house.

Clermont was sold by Jane and Lucy Chomley in 1894 by auction. My father bid for it, but it was bought by Col Tottenham. Afterwards, he did not want it and let my father have it for the price he had paid. Francis Chomley had died, and his two sisters were very old ladies who had lived in great poverty. They were not on speaking terms and one old lady lived up in the drawing room and the room off it, and the other in the dining room and the study, with an old woman who attended on them living in the basement.

Clermont was a large square house, in bad state of repair. When we went there, it was reroofed and entirely done up, both within and without, and the coachman’s house rebuilt. There was an open area all around the house. In the N.W. corner of the area, there was a broad flight of five stone steps leading up to a path which ran through a shrubbery to the pond. There was also a large shrubbery on the south side which contained a dry closet with seven seats! (This was still in situ when Clermont was sold; a fine example of early 18th century architecture)”.

There seems little doubt that the Youghal incident affected not only BAS himself and his career, but the whole family; in particular, the sons. Bunt was then 5 years old, Jim 3, and Alan 2, while Pat and Regi were not yet born. By the time the family moved to Wicklow a year or two later, one would have expected BAS to have started thinking about schools. Regi did say that Bunt and Jim had some schooling in Dublin – perhaps between 1892 and 1894 when they were at Harcourt Street. The others had none. There was a succession of governesses and tutors; Miss Shillaker, Miss Tedder (aunt of the head of the RAF ?), Miss Atwood and others; Mr Burks and others. The story is that he thought schools were cruel; one can imagine the difficulties the young boys did/would have faced with their father having been deemed responsible for the Youghal incident. Irish memories are notoriously long. Toby Truell alledged that he thought schools were ‘smutty’ places ! While the sons carried their individual difficulties into adulthood in their different ways, the girls were not really affected as governesses and the lady like arts they taught were the norm.

BAS was a skilled carpenter; and skilled generally with his hands. He was also one of the really fine early photographers, with his own dark room, and left a fine photographic legacy of about 500 plates, quarter, half and full size; these survive as an important ‘Country House’ collection – save for those taken out by Cecil and her family and not returned !

BAS was extremely ‘low church’ and had a highly developed sense of right and wrong. This may have contributed to the decision to educate the children at home. Nonetheless, he is reputed to have sacked a governess for having a cross on her prayer book. He hated the way in which women chatted after church services, considering gossip as highly dangerous. Regi said he ceased to attend church towards the end of his life for that reason. The family grave at Wicklow, in which he is buried, has no cross and doesn’t bear his name.

He encouraged his children in a wide variety of sports; hockey was the most important game, with teams being formed between Clermont and the neighbouring houses, Bluebottles and Scarlet Runners, but tennis and, even golf, were also encouraged. BAS, with others, including Morgan Crofton of Inchinappa, founded the Wicklow Golf Club on the Blainroe road; photographs of the family are to be seen in the Club house. Field sports were equally encouraged; fishing on the Vartry lakes and at Doyles on Lough Dan, shooting at Clermont, on the Lakes and at Clonmannon, ferrets were kept for the sport, and the family went otter hunting at Avoca and Woodenbridge, by train !

BAS was, of course, renowned in the family as the first member to take an interest in genealogy, not only in the Somerville family, but many others as well, both connected and not. The Somerville Records, consisting of carefully annotated indexed books, inter family letters, diaries, bibles, pedigrees, declarations and memoranda survive. The importance of them cannot be overestimated; all of them being researched and written before the disastrous fire in the Public Record Office during the Civil War where so many parish registers were destroyed. Many of these Records formed the base from which Cecil built up the genealogical papers comprised in the Rooke Papers now in the National Library. BAS’ interest started at an early age and continued throughout his life; reference has been made to his first pedigree; his last is a beautifully illustrated masterpiece, tracing the family back from the early 20th century to the 11th century, albeit, there is one acknowledged error discovered with further research and one hundred years have passed since it was made ! It fits into a fine oak box and winds down like a blind; it was formerly fixed above the double doors between the study and billiard room at Clermont.
Apart from BAS’ genealogical, photographic and aesthetic legacies at Clermont, he must be

credited, together with his wife Dick, with lifting the family from the pedestrian life of the early and mid 19th century. The junior branch of the family had gradually descended to a lower social status during the first 70 years of the 19th century. While the senior branch had married heiresses in several generations which helped them enlarge and maintain their properties, and secure their social life and careers, the junior branch had not. BAS made use of such contacts as he had and with the fortune finally brought in by his wife at the end of the century, secured the family for a further generation.

Sadly, BAS continued to suffer ill health, even while building up the property at Clermont. He developed some disease that interfered with his balance (Reynier’s disease ? ); he retired from any form of social life; Regi said he was terrified people would think he had been drinking, which would offend his sense of morality. He died of flu in January 1916.
WBRBS from conversation with Regi and from the Somerville Records.

Bellingham Arthur Somerville followed his father into the Royal Irish Constabulary in 1872 at the age of 18. He married Margaret Hall Clinch of a prominent banking and brewing family from Witney, Oxfordshire on 27 Aug 1879. The 1891 census finds him living at The Elms, Witney. He is just 36 years old and gives his profession as a District Inspector, Royal Irish Constabulary (Retired).

Investigations into his RIC record (see below) reveal that he wasn’t the best of police officers and he left the service in 1891. He was, however, admitted to the Freedom of the City of Dublin in May 1893.
The family moved to Clermont in 1895 which he extended by building the assymetrical wings. Undoubtedly, the property would have looked much better had they matched.
He was a director of Clinch and Co brewery. We know he was very interested in family history and between 1874 and
1915 gathered and archived information relating to the Somervilles from parish records, certificates, genaeological
magazines, the Dublin Record Office, British Museum, churches, letters and libraries. This later formed the basis of the
Somerville Index produced by Cecilia Rooke (nee Somerville), his eldest daughter.

In 1874 Bellingham Arthur Somerville had been reprimanded for failing to pay his men on time and in 1878 we find him ‘under supervision’ for ‘pecuniary embarrassments’. Sometime early in 1887 he was sent to Youghal, Cork where, following a misconceived attempt to arrest a local Catholic priest, a number of protestors gathered in an incident on Tuesday 8th March which then began to turn ugly. It seems that during the subsequent riot Somerville ordered his men to fix bayonets and charge at the stone-throwing mob. A fisherman called Patrick Hanlon was stabbed in the back and killed. The Police Constable responsible, a man named Ward, and District Inspector Somerville were held in custody while the matter was investigated.

At the coroner’s enquiry it emerged that a telegram had been sent to Youghal police with instructions to “Deal very summarily if any organized resistance to lawful authority. If necessary do not hesitate to shoot them.” Nevertheless, on 23 March 1887, a majority of 13 jurors out of a total of 18 signed a verdict which declared: ‘Constable Ward is guilty of murder. We also find Inspector Somerville guilty of willful murder by having aided, abetted and encouraged him to commit the act..’

The Attorney General for Ireland faced questions in the House of Commons immediately and the repercussions resounded for some months. PC Ward and DI Somerville were released on bail on 30 March having posted surety of £50 and £500 respectively. This is the equivalent of £4,300 and £43,000 in 2010 prices. Both men were suspended from the Irish Constabulary.

Eventually, in Sept 1887, it was decided not to prosecute – even today it is rare to see a police officer put on trial - and both Ward and Somerville returned to duty. Although Somerville had been declared guilty of willful murder by a jury he was never able to clear his name.

By November 1887 Somerville, “of Youghal notoriety” as The Times put it, had been removed to Wicklow. He continued to work for another 4 years as a 1st Class Sub-Inspector before taking retirement with an annual pension of £111 (approx £10,000 in today’s prices).
Written and researched by David Gilmour
Sources: Royal Irish Constabulary records and The Times archives.
