Vere Frances de Merlie Bellingham Somerville(0678)

I have seen the notes in the Truell profile and comment as follows. The brewery was founded by John Williams Clinch, William Clinch’s father, indeed, possibly his father, I can check in the yard in due course; I will provide more information on this when I go into papers more deeply. I know there was the bank and several farms. There was also a brewery at Onchan in the Isle of Man, which had some connection. I don’t know the number of the house in Hollywell which had the school. I had heard the story about the gold coin and the bank. I didn’t realize she had been engaged twice before meeting BAS. The reason for going to the UK was her English patriotism, I am told; she evidently did say “my country needs me”. The reason Jack Clinch was disinherited was because he drank and, therefore, could not be involved in the management of the business. )

Margaret Hall Clinch was called Daisy before she was married and signed the series of four watercolours she painted as a teenager ‘Daisy Clinch’. After her marriage, she was always referred to by her husband BAS (0631) as ‘Dick’ and named that way in the catalogue of glass plates wherever she appears.

Daisy went to a school in Hollywell, in Oxford; Holywell runs parallel to the High Street, north of New College, leading from Broad Street to Long Wall Street. It is said that the school was unusually strict; she seemed to excel in the usual arts of that time. Examples of her needlework survived until recently, and some of her fine watercolours still do.

Erina Somerville(named Cis by her siblings, Aunt Amy by her nephews and nieces) went to the same school and was escorted on the journeys by one of her brothers, Henry or BAS. Daisy was engaged to be married to a Eugene de Ritson at an early age, but, on meeting BAS, broke it off. Amy and BAS went to stay in Witney with the Clinches between Monday 7 January 1878 and Sunday 3 February 1878 on which date BAS’ diary records he returned and “came back an engaged man having been engaged to Mr and Mrs Clinch’s second daughter Margaret Hall”.

After their wedding at Witney in August 1879, BAS and Daisy honeymooned in Paris; they returned to BAS’ District in Newtownards, Co Down. Thereafter they moved around the country wherever BAS was appointed, staying in rented accommodation until he retired, early through sickness, in 1891 at which point they were living at Friars Hill in Wicklow, BAS’ last District. They then seemed to have lived for perhaps two years in 82, Harcourt Street in Dublin while deciding where to go; by 1894, they were back in the Wicklow area renting Ballyhenry House near Ashford (1894) and Seaview in Wicklow(1895). BAS had bought Clermont in Rathnew in 1894, which required extensive renovation and improvement, so they continued to rent until they moved in in early 1895.

The regime at Clermont was strict. Children could only have either butter or jam; never both. Later on, men had one sausage; women half a sausage. Dick was extremely careful; look after the pennies, the pounds will look after themselves. Children were educated at home by governesses and tutors. Amusements were devised by themselves; hockey, tennis and rounders offered the only opportunity to meet outsiders. The boys enjoyed shooting and, down on the lakes, fishing and wild fowling. A stuffed sparrow hawk and kestrel, shot by Regi, when fourteen, stand on a shelf behind the writer.

Both BAS and Dick, as she was now known, suffered from ill health, on and off. He continued to have some sickness that had bothered him throughout his career; and within about 15 years he began to withdraw from meeting any outsiders at all. Regi said he used to stagger and fall( Reyniers Disease ?) and he was careful that he should not be seen lest it be thought he had been drinking. At the wedding of one of his daughters in 1912, he would not attend and in the wedding photograph, taken on the upper terrace, he is to be seen in the study window looking on. (WBRBS has this photograph and will identify the daughter when it comes to hand). Dick contracted Anthrax – how, it is not known; thereafter, from her photographs, she seemed to lack her former sparkle.

After BAS’ death in 1916, Dick lived on at Clermont. The car was stolen, with Langrell at the wheel, during the Troubles. When the IRA returned it, they were summoned to the drawing room and dressed down by the fearless lady of the house, who struck terror into the gunmen, proudly asserted that she was English, that her sons were all at the front and secured some form of undertaking that they and the family would not be targeted when they returned. It was customary for young army officers to be shot if found at home. Regi was ambushed on his motor bike at the top of Ballinabarney in 1916, before he went to the front, in the belief he was Pat.

After WW1 Dick travelled extensively; several times to India where the three elder boys, and Tetty and John either were, or had been, and twice to Regi in Kenya. The letters which David Gilmour has provided make it all seem as if the journeys of more than a month were a brief trip down the road !

After the second World War, when Clermont was closed and Dick was in England, sometimes in London, sometimes Oxford, sometimes Birmingham, she returned to Ireland and played weekly Bridge with Aileen Crofton of Inchinappa, Dottie Tottenham of Ballycurry, Henry and Patsy Truell of Clonmannon and others. It was a ritual; the teas were, to a small onlooker, scrumptious, but the regime had a distinct formality about it. The ritual for Wednesdays and Sundays between 1946 and 1949 was a trip down to the garden in the wheelchair, covered in a dun coloured corduroy material, and back again, Regi in control accompanied by Regi’s family when at home. The reward was the cream; even though on the turn for want of hygiene in the dairy. Dick was quite stern; she stared and tended to frighten people. She had a disconcerting habit of watching people eat; and constantly reprimanded Juanita for drinking her milk too quickly. It is difficult to imagine warmth; yet her letters are certainly warm and affectionate. At home she was conscious of her position as a ‘grande dame’, with a companion, but always in control herself. She held the keys of the store room to the day of her death. Bunt had tried to persuade her to sell Clermont after the war when there was a ready market among English people escaping the Labour Government and its hair shirt policies; no, I would seem a pauper !.

Dick was much respected by the locals. During WW1, she had provided help in one form or another to a sorely distressed village. It is said that she paid the wages of everyman who volunteered until the first pay cheque came through from the War Office. Rathnew and Newtown Mt Kennedy sent more men to the front, per head of population, than any other in the British Isles. This, however, was more a sign of the economic conditions of the time than of patriotism; nonetheless, the gentry provided example, both in those whom they sent out, and in the good works of those at home.
Dick died of pneumonia, the great killer of those times, in July 1949, shortly before her 90th birthday.

She was buried in the same grave, at Rathnew Cemetery, as her infant Truell grandchildren, rather than with BAS in Wicklow Churchyard as she had a fear of being buried over water. The church and churchyard at Wicklow are situated high above the Vartry River just before it enters Wicklow Harbour and the sea. A few years ago (2011) a portion of the eastern side of the churchyard suffered a landslide and collapsed down towards the river. The Somerville grave is at the western side. The name of the area near Rathnew, where the cemetery is situated, is called ‘Merrymeetings’. Irish funerals tend to be far larger than those in England. The funeral cortege, comprised of the people of Rathnew, filled the road from Clermont on the north side to Merrymeetings on the south side.
Dick’s memory lived on in Rathnew for many years.
WBRBS from personal knowledge and conversations with Regi, Honor and Dorothy Rooke; and from the Somerville Records.

We have just passed through the Straits of Messina – it was very beautiful – there were a certain number of soft clouds + some mist in places, with bright sunshine in other parts & on the sea this was a joyful blue- and is still – which all added to the glory of it – at 4 o/c this morning a number of us got up to see Stromboli – which was in slight eruption. I could not have imagined anything like it – the huge tongues of flame boiling + boiling up, then a great burst which threw enormous boulders of lava up into the air which then poured down the side of the mountain – only to be followed by another burning stream. We were quite near to it all + at the time it was dark which added very much to the effect. I could never have imagined it and would not have missed it for anything. I only wished that some of you could have been here to enjoy it with me. It is much warmer now, we have a shiny soft wind – with bright sunshine – we could not wish for a more perfect day but I cannot thoroughly enjoy it without some of my dear ones with me. I cannot “warm” to strangers & there are only a very few on the boat who can talk to. Sometimes I go to see Mrs French & very much enjoy a gossip with her. I try to take some exercise walking round the deck - ten times is a mile – which I am afraid I never accomplish - & in the middle of the day it is impossible to walk – it is so crowded – we have only the one deck for every one and every thing: for games have to be got in somehow & we have over 90 children on board - at times the noise is deafening – then I go to my cabin for a little quiet – it is impossible to get it on deck. Some of the passengers wanted to get up to sports but had to give up the idea as there is no room – very often they cannot have here “deck tennis” – there is really [illegible] deck. I know in the 3rd class theirs have – but that is their only advantage – otherwise I should not care for it.

This is another joyful day but there is decidedly a strong roll – yesterday it was very rough – many of the passengers & most of the children felt it badly. I am thankful to say it makes no difference to me, except that it is very difficult to move about one falls over things. It calmed down in the day so I went and had a long gossip with Mrs French which I much enjoyed – she gives me so much information, about farming and their life in Kenya – it is all very much the same as Uncle Regi has let me into further details – she is beginning to look very tired and how it is hard work taking charge of their two little children on the boat when [illegible possibly ‘finding’] it is so difficult to manage & she has to do all the washing for them too as there is no laundry on board.

Will you ask mother, when she is down the town, if she will go to Barts and tell them to send me a tube of Borafax. I forgot to buy it – there is no hurry and I have plenty to last for some time, but I just like to have it by me - ask her to let me know what she pays – including postage - & I will give it to her later on.

We ought to arrive at Port Said every early in this evening, we have to do some [illegible] there but they say it will not take long. If we only stay short time I shall not go ashore – there is nothing to interest me there and I [illegible - ‘think on the boat one has to luncheon’ ?]
Will you give my best love to all darling child & keep a big share for yourself.

Borafax was a skin cream which is no longer on the market. It was made with boric acid, a weak anti-fungal,anti-biotic, and might have been used in case of bites or perhaps as an early form of sun cream. (source: internet)
I feel more than guilty for not having answered your [illeg] nice letter long ago – somehow there is always so much to be done - + then one puts off writing.
I hear you had a wonderful holiday and then finished up at Swanage with the family, how you much have thoroughly enjoyed it all + I hear the change has done everyone good.

We have had Uncle Pat here for eight days – he had to leave on Wednesday evening for a course of lectures we wanted to attend in London – he is staying there now – he is looking better + I though him very much improved during the few days he was here – I just loved having him.
I am very much looking forward to seeing you all next month and hope to be with you midday on the 13th as Tettie + I cross now into Liverpool – she will [illeg] to London.
We are getting very busy now – there seems so much to be done before long – I cannot get through a great deal in the day - I get so tired.

Your dear Mother’s letter to Tettie arrived this morning – we were very glad to hear of you all – I expect you are busy at term-time again – I thought of you on Thursday morning starting off to College.
My love to you all + a big big share for your dear self,
Saturday Since early yesterday morning it has been very rough & delayed as to such we do not get to Port Said until after 9 o/c tonight. G

Here we are rushing now as fast as we can towards the East. We spent all Tuesday at Marseilles. Such crowds on the pier when we arrived, any amount of [..ing] , [.. ing] , selling fruit, music dancing + singing – all most amusing to watch. [illeg] + I took a short taxi drive through the town – just to see something of it – unfortunately all the shops were closed as it was All Saints Day – but we enjoyed the drive and it was very nice to get away from the ship for a short time – it is a very tiring life on board – always a [illeg] + bustle – there are so many moving about – it is quite impossible to get any real rest and there are children playing + [illeg] in every direction. Night is about as loud as day for there is dancing going on for a long time + cabin is small + very hot now we have the third person in it. She is somewhat large and an American – but she really tries to be nice + we quite like her, although we can’t help wishing to have the place to ourselves - In spite of all [illeg] I am feeling much better and really far more rested than when I left home.

For a few hours this morning, it tried to rain though it soon gave up the attempt which was the only time since we left Gib. Early yesterday morning we went thought the Straits of Bonifacio it was awfully pretty and very early this evening we went through the straits of Messina – We are due at Port Said on Saturday morning & expect to be there about 4 hours – after that we do not put in anywhere until we get to Bombay – so there will not be another chance of writing until then- we are due there on the 15th.

This day three weeks ago I arrived with you at Cheltenham – How I enjoyed those few days – it seems years ago – Please remember me to Grandpapa. My very best love to you all - + I shall think of you so much – but you must not trouble to write to me until the [illeg] when I should [illeg – love?] a letter.
PS. Please tell Mother I am wishing for the best of the [games?].

This morning I received your letter – it was so good of you to write to me when your time must be very much taken up with so many parties & other amusements and I am sure you want every spare moment to help mother who must have had a tremendous amount to do with Michael so ill and in [illeg] – I don’t know how she was able to write to me – it was sweet of her – her last weeks’ letter was delayed but I got the two today, - the [illeg – news?] cheered me wonderfully to find above all that Michael was better – and things settling down. You must have had a very very slow winter, I am quite sure you enjoyed the snow + ice – personally I dislike it very much and have always preferred warm weather – when we can get about so much easier and enjoy the country – which I love.

It has been quite cold here, it is gradually getting warmer – and we are now able to sit out in the middle of the day – every afternoon this week we have been watching a tennis tournament the finals will be tomorrow – then we get another better tournament which will be most interesting. On the 13th the Horse Show begins. We shall then get a good polo tournament. I think I enjoy watching polo more than anything. It is wonderful to see the ponies watching the ball – they appear quite as keen about it all as their riders – then it is so thrilling when they are galloping for all they are worth along the ground.

I have heard from Aunt Kitty that she is going home this year instead of their [inlaws] She is sailing with “China” on the 21ST of March so I have arranged to go to Secundarabad on the 1ST March until the 15th: when I go on to Bombay & Tettie will meet me there – she will stay here while I am at Secunderabad. This will give to about twelve days there & about the same at Bombay.

I believe it is already quite hot in Bombay – and they have had to start fans - [illeg]... Tettie & i hope to rush up to [illeg] for me just to see the [illeg]. We shall probably only stay there one night, which will really give us two days there – it will be quite enough to see all we want.

I suppose you are now back at College and hard at work again – I have met out here a good many old Cheletenham College girls who always love to talk about it – and of course it is tremendously interesting to me.
I hear Major Hume is now in Delhi in the [illeg].I have not yet met him – he probably has not care to see anyone which is quite natural. I am more than sorry for him – it must all have been terrible.

I hear Billy [B___] is to go back to school again this tern – I should think it is much & happier for him – he seemed quite a “lost sheep” at home by himself – I am most thankful he is going – t[illeg] + Girlie seems to be a great deal better too.

I am writing this very hurriedly and there are people in and out – this is the worst of things on a Veranda, one can never get a really quiet time – everybody seems to know what you are doing + what you have + one hardly seems to have any real work to do – it may be well enough for a short time but it would be too dreadful to spend one’s life in this way – and have nothing to look back to – but regrets for wasted time .
Give my love to all – especially Mother - + keep lots for yourself darling Child

Many many happy returns of your birthday darling Child – I hope you will have every blessing + that life will be a joy to you and that your will help to make it the same for all your dear ones - & this prepare you for greater happiness afterwards.
You have made such a splendid effort to do what is right – go on darling in the same way + it will bring you such happiness.
I am sending you a little present with my very best love – I hope you will like it + when you wear it, you will be reminded of the good wishes + fond love of your old

Elizabeth Jane Caulfeild (born June 21, 1834 – died at Roxborough Castle, Moy, County Tyrone, Ireland, May 31, 1882). She was the only daughter of William Meredyth, first Lord Athlumney, and by marriage in December 1856 to James Caulfeild, 3rd Earl of Charlemont, she became the Countess of Charlemont.

Although a Christian by upbringing, she became a regular attendant at synagogue worship, often seeking advice in spiritual matters from rabbis. Lady Charlemont resided in the country near Belfast, the synagogue of which town she frequently attended; while in London she worshipped at the services of the Bayswater and Central synagogues. She was a woman of varied accomplishments, an excellent linguist, and a good musician. She possessed a remarkable gift for recitation, which she utilized on behalf of charitable institutions.
References: This article incorporates text from the 1901–1906 Jewish Encyclopedia, a publication now in the public domain.

Roxborough Castle was built some time in the 18th century, probably by the 1st Earl of Charlemont. In the middle of the 19th century the 2nd and 3rd Earls carried out extensive renovations and rebuilding to produce a large French-style chateau. The house was set on fire in 1922. Only the elaborate 19th century gates and screen survive.

Roxborough Castle was a plain 5 bay block of 3 storeys over a high basement was enlarged and remodelled from 1842 onwards by 2nd Earl; his architect being William Murray. Wings were added of 1 bay and 2 storeys over a basement, running the full length of the original block; these were in Murray's rather restrained Italianate style; the original block being given triangular window pediments and similar features so as to match them. The entrance was moved round to the side of of one of these wings, which became the new entrance front; of 3 bays with a low portico. At the other side of the house, a large office court was built; a feature of which was a row of 4 little octagons with pyramidal roofs, described in the plan as 'larders'. The entrance door under the portico opened into a hall at basement level, from which a flight of steps led to a vestibule in the main block of the house, with the staircase opening off it at one side. The space saved by moving the entrance to the wing enabled a new large drawing room to be formed in the original block; but the proportions of the other two principal rooms, the dining room and library, remained unchanged. Some time in the C19 the rooms were adorned with chimneypieces and doors brought from Charlemont House in Dublin. Ca 1864, soon after the third earl inherited, the house was radically transformed by the young 'eclectic' architect William J Barre. Murray's wings were rebuilt on a much larger scale so that they became 3 storeys high and projected on either side of the original block. The ends of the wings were treated as corner towers or pavilions and given high Mansard roofs in the French chateau manner, crowned with decorative ironwork; but in a typically Victorian way, one of these roofs was made slightly different from the other 3. The skyline was further enlivened with pointed and pinnacled dormers, tall chimneystacks with segmental caps, and a row of steep little pediments like saw teeth along the roof cornice. There were similar but larger pediments over the downstairs windows, some of them interlocking and with tympana containing carved heads representing members of the Charlemont family, their ancestors and several of the leading political personages of the day. Barre's exterior ornamentation of his new wings defies description; his biographer, writing 1868, a year after his untimely death, describes it as 'the very extensive use of Classic and Gothic detail indiscrminately, an immediate connection with each other'. All this ornament was confined to the wings, the original block remaining much as Murray had left it; except for the addition of a porch, not centrally placed, on one of its fronts; the entrance having been moved here from the wing. The whole effect was spectacular, if somewhat reminiscent of the Grand Hotel at a fashionable Victorian resort.

Motorists passing through the village of Moy can stop in Charlemont at the junction to Portadown and see the cast-iron gate and screen set up in the 19th century to provide the grand entrance to the Castle. The richly modelled metalwork is thought by some to have been the work of the firm of the celebrated Dublin iron-founder Richard Turner, best known for his conservatories in Dublin, Belfast and Kew Gardens. 200 yards further along towards Armagh, right on the corner, one can still see the gates and ruins of the gate house to the Fort.

Sir James Molyneux Caulfeild, 3rd Earl of Charlemont KP (6 October 1820 – 12 January 1892) was an Irish politician and peer.
He was the son of Hon. Henry Caulfeild and Elizabeth Margaret Browne. Lord Charlemont married on two occasions;
Hon. Elizabeth Jane Somerville, daughter of William Meredyth Somerville, 1st Baron Meredyth and Lady Maria Harriet Conyngham, on 18 December 1856.
Anna Lucy Lambart, daughter of Reverend Charles James Lambart and Marian Smith, on 10 May 1883 at the British Consulate, Pau, France.

Charlemont was educated at Trinity College, Cambridge. He was appointed High Sheriff of Armagh for 1842 and held the office of Liberal Member of Parliament (MP) for County Armagh between 1847 and 1857. He was Lord Lieutenant of County Armagh between 1849 and 1864.

He succeeded to the title of 3rd Earl of Charlemont, amongst the other peerages, on 26 December 1863. He held the office of Lord Lieutenant of County Tyrone between 1864 and 1892. He was invested as a Knight of St Patrick on 28 December 1865.
He died in Biarritz, France and was buried in St Patrick's Cathedral, Armagh.

Henry Boan (1860-1941), retailer and sportsman, was born on 4 November 1860 at Jones Creek near Dunolly, Victoria, son of Thomas Boan, miner and road contractor, and his wife Rachel, née Isaacs. Sketchily educated at Dunolly, where his English-born parents had settled in the 1850s after some time in California, United States of America, he left his poor but secure Jewish home at 16 to work as a messenger in Flegeltaub's Ballarat warehouse for 10s. a week and keep. Promoted to town-traveller at £2 10s. a week, he soon resigned, failed to find a niche in Melbourne and, after working his way to Sydney, lived a hand-to-mouth existence. Posts in mercantile houses like Anthony Hordern's and David Jones's were lost from pride and impulsiveness. For four years he drifted from job to job in Sydney, Brisbane, Toowoomba, Charters Towers and elsewhere, and was often penniless.

Harry Boan never lost faith in his ability or prospects, and in 1886 his parents offered him their £200 savings to make a fresh start. With his brother Ernest, he opened a store in booming Broken Hill. His imaginative buying and advertising soon produced a turnover of £1000 a week. Expanding steadily, Boan Bros was soon the leading drapery establishment of the 'Silver City'. In the mid-1890s Broken Hill was crippled by strikes; in 1895 Harry sold out to his brother and migrated with another brother Benjamin to Western Australia, where gold-fever had created an expanding market. The site selected for their store was marginal and swampy, but was directly opposite the central railway station. Despite a chronic shortage of labour and materials and the need to borrow £62,000, a single-storey building was erected within four months. On 17 June 1896 in Sydney, with Hebrew rites, Harry married Sophie, daughter of the merchant Barnett Bebarfald; they had four children.

Boan had a fine physique, a neat beard and a distinguished manner. He dressed smartly, talked fluently and well, and loved an audience. His promotional methods startled parochial Perth. When Boan Bros opened on 7 November 1895 it almost sold out, and had to close for a day to replenish stock and recruit a hundred more assistants. By the 1920s it was called 'the people's store'; free trains and taxis brought customers to and from its birthday-sales. Though much was spent on lifts and other facilities, little went on frills and the floor-boards remained bare. Local enterprise was encouraged by special promotion of Western Australian goods, and a factory was established to service the store.

Benjamin's death in 1901 gave Harry sole control, and he bought land adjoining the store in 1910. Before expanding through to Murray Street next year, he toured Europe and America, seeking ideas. About 1913 his wife and children settled in England; henceforth he lived alone in Perth hotels.

Boan was elected unopposed to the Legislative Council in April 1917, but resigned suddenly in February 1918 after criticism of the opening in his store of a branch of the State Savings Bank. Soon afterwards, he floated the store as a limited company, left for England, living in Park Lane, London, and at Cobham, Surrey. In July 1919 at the Guards' Chapel, his second daughter married the earl of Athlumney, an Irish peer. In 1928 his elder daughter, widowed in World War I, married Lieutenant P. G. Agnew, R.N., who was created a baronet in 1957. Returning to Perth about 1920 Boan was re-elected to the Legislative Council as a Nationalist candidate in November 1922; he did not renominate in 1924.

Politics seemingly bored him, but horses, both on the turf and in the hunting-field, were a consuming passion. He was a fine judge of horseflesh and his racing stud brought him many trophies: Tanami cost him £300 and won over £5000, including the Australian Jockey Club Derby of 1910, while Maltfield won £1750 and Maltblossom £1250. He took a close paternal interest in the Children's Hospital, served as president of its board and made frequent generous donations.

Following the death of an elder son who had been intended to succeed him, Boan gladly relinquished control of the store to his son Frank who returned from England late in 1929. By about 1932 Harry turned to serious horse-breeding and racing, and settled in Melbourne near a brother and sister. He died at Caulfield of chronic heart and kidney conditions on 18 March 1941, and was buried in Karrakatta cemetery, Perth, with Anglican rites.

“Rochfort House (which later became known as Tudenham House) was built next door to Belvedere and was a far larger and superior house. Robert, who was consumed with anger and jealousy over his brother’s fine mansion, had a wall built between the two houses, blocking his view of his brother’s residence. This wall, the largest folly ever built in Ireland, standing three storeys high and over 180 feet long, became known as ‘The Jealous Wall’.

“By the time Robert Rochfort died in 1744 he had acquired the nickname ‘‘The Wicked Earl’ and it was said he was murdered for all his wicked deeds. When his wife was finally released from captivity, old and haggard, she fled to France, became a nun and spent the remainder of her life as a hermit.

“No children were ever born at Belvedere. The house was passed from cousin to cousin: Charles Kenneth Howard-Bury owned it in 1912 and from Charles it was handed to Rex Beaumont in 1963. In 1982 Westmeath County Council bought the estate for £250,000, the house was restored and is now open to the public.”

“Tudenham House, built by George Rochfort in 1742, was first called Rochfort House. Rochfort employed the architect Richard Castle, who had also designed George’s brother’s house next door, Belvedere House.
“Rochfort House was a very fine three-storey house, seven bays at the front with a central niche and oculus and seven bays on each of the sides which featured central curved bows.

The front doorway led into a great hall with columns at both ends. Four large reception rooms with fine plasterwork, a library, billiard room and gun room were accessed from the hall. The two-storey upper hall had a large dome which was reglazed with stained glass in the nineteenth century. Eight bedrooms and a bathroom were found on the first floor and the top floor held a further suite of bedrooms.
The vaulted basement was immense, with a huge kitchen and the servants’ quarters. The Rochfort estate amounted to over 850 acres.

“Rochfort House was sold in the Landed Estates Court in 1836 and bought by Sir Francis Hopkins, second Baronet of Athboy. Sir Francis renamed the property Tudenham House. He died in 1860 and left the house to his sister, Anna Maria, who was married to Nicholas Loftus Tottenham. Anna Maria built a new front lodge to the house, and moved the driveway, making it exactly one mile long.”

He continues: “During the First World War the house was used as a hospital. Charles Tottenham died in 1929 leaving his wife, Georgina, as the head of the household. Charles’s son Harold returned from South Africa and occupied Tudenham for some years but the enormous house was very difficult to maintain. Harold extended the garden cottage and made it into a comfortable family home.

“During the Second World War the house was occupied by the Irish Army. After the war the house was unused. Eventually in 1957 anything of use was removed: doors, wall coverings, fireplaces and furniture all found new homes. The roof was removed and the house left as an empty shell. The Tudenham estate was taken over by the Land Commission, which divided it into five farms, which were then let to various tenants.
“Abandoned Mansions of Ireland”, published by The Collins Press

Sir Charles Stanley Monck, 4th Viscount Monck

Governor of British North America (1861 - 1867) and Governor General after Confederation (1867 - 1868) Appointed Canada's first Governor General: June 1, 1867 Sworn In: July 1, 1867, Ottawa, Ontario Born: October 10, 1819, Templemore, Ireland Died: November 29, 1894

Viscount Monck was Canada's first Governor General – but he had actually served as Governor of British North America since 1861. Lord Monck worked hard to build Confederation. His efforts to unite and stabilize the young country were recognized with his appointment to the position of Canada's first Governor General in 1867.

In 1861, when Lord Monck first arrived in his official post, there were simmering tensions between Canada and the republic to the south. Then, 20 days before he took office on November 28, the "Trent Affair" erupted – a diplomatic crisis between Britain and the United States government that threatened to use Canada as its battleground – and war seemed inevitable. In the course of his term, Lord Monck used his influence to diffuse the explosive potential not only of this crisis, but of many others to follow.

Lord Monck's skill as a diplomat in Canadian-American relations was matched by his ability in promoting Confederation. He helped build "The Great Coalition", the consolidation of the Reform and Conservative parties that was key to the colonies' pursuit of federalism. In Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, he was a tireless promoter of unity and played a leading role in the preparations for a federal union.

In a visit to the new capital in 1864, Lord Monck saw Rideau Hall, which became the Governor General's residence, and was purchased by the Government of Canada from the MacKay estate in 1868 for $82,000. Before living in Ottawa, the Moncks had resided at Spencerwood, near Quebec City. However, even after moving to Rideau Hall, getting to the heart of Ottawa was still no easy matter. The battered condition of the roads often resulted in Lord Monck travelling to Parliament by canopied boat up the Ottawa River.
Lady Monck loved horticulture and made considerable improvements to the grounds of the official residence.

Viscount Monck was a private man who enjoyed the company of family and close friends. Those who knew him well spoke of his courtesy, kindness and wit. "I like him amazingly", wrote John A. MacDonald of Monck, "and shall be very sorry when he leaves, as he has been a very prudent and efficient administrator of public affairs.
Life Before and After Rideau Hall

Prior to being appointed as Governor General of Canada, Charles Stanley Monck graduated from Trinity College in Dublin, Ireland with a degree in law and became a Member of Parliament in the House of Commons in England in 1852. In 1844, he married Lady Elizabeth Louise Mary Monck and they had seven children, four of whom lived to adulthood. Lord Monck was raised to the peerage of Ireland as 4th Viscount Monck and Baron Monck of Ballytrammon, county Wexford, on April 20, 1849, upon the death of his father, and in 1866, he was created a peer of the United Kingdom as 4th Viscount Monck and Baron Monck of Ballytrammon, county Wexford, in the United Kingdom. Lord Monck was appointed Lord of the Treasury in the Palmerston government between 1855 and 1857.

When his term of office ended on November 14, 1868, he returned directly to Ireland. He served as Lord Lieutenant of County Dublin from 1874 to 1892. Lady Monck died on June 16, 1892, and Lord Monck on November 29, 1894.

She applied in 1924 to the Ulster King of Arms for a formal Grant of Arms, in the form carried by the family since the time of James the Planter, for the descendants of Major William Somerville, second son of Sir James Somerville of the City of Dublin, Baronet, M.P., she being the only child of Henry Bellingham Somerville. ‘Whereas application hath been made unto me by Elizabeth Mary Somerville of 74 Morehampton Road in the City of Dublin, only child of Henry Bellingham Somerville, District Inspector Royal Irish Constabulary, who was the great grandson of William Somerville, Major in His Majesty’s Army, second son of Sir James Somerville of the City of Dublin, Baronet, M.P. ………………Know ye therefore that I, the said Ulster King of Arms …….do ratify, exemplify and confirm unto the said Elizabeth Mary Somerville and the other descendants of her ancestor the said William Somerville, Major in His Majesty’s Army, the Arms following that is to say: Azure, three mullets or, two and one between seven cross crosslets fitchee, argent, three, one, two and one, for Crest, on a wreath of the colours, A demi lion rampant sable, charged on the shoulder with a cross crosslet fitchee and two mullets argent, mantled gules doubled argent, and for Motto, Crains Dieu tant que tu viveras, the same as in the margent is more clearly depicted ……In Witness whereof I subscribe these presents with my Name and Title and affix hereunto the Seal of my Office this second day of April in the Fourtenth year of the Reign of our Sovereign Lord George the Fifth, by the Grace of God of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland and of the British Dominions beyond the Seas, King, Defender of the Faith and so forth, and in the year of Our Lord One thousand nine hundred and twenty four. (Signed) Neville Wilkinson – Ulster – King of Arms of All Ireland.’
The Grant was entered in the Register of Ulster’s Office in ‘Grants and Confirmations’ Vol.M. folio 44.

SOMERVILLE, Lt-Col William Arthur Tennison Bellingham

Born 8 Aug. 1882; s of late Bellingham Arthur Somerville and Margaret, y d of late William Clinch; m 1925, Amy Kathleen, widow of Alan Campbell Ferguson and d of General Standish Harrison, Castle Harrison, Charleville, Co. Cork; died 13 Feb. 1951
late the King’s Own Royal Regiment (Lancaster)
Entered Army, 1901; Captain, 1913; Major, 1916; European War, 1914–18; N. Russia, 1919 (despatches nine times, DSO and bar, Bt Lt-Col); commanding 1st Batt. Loyal Regt, 1927–28; retired pay, 1928

‘SOMERVILLE, Lt-Col William Arthur Tennison Bellingham’, Who Was Who, A & C Black, 1920–2008; online edn, Oxford University Press, Dec 2007 [http://www.ukwhoswho.com/view/article/oupww/whowaswho/U243165, accessed 12 July 2011]

Late in 1919 Britain sent troops to Murmansk and Archangel in northern Russia. They were part of an international force designed to protect Allied interests there during the Russian Civil War, and to offer assistance to those Russian forces fighting the Bolsheviks in that conflict.

8th Battalion Machine Gun Corps was based at Dibgate, Shorncliffe on the 30th March 1919 and was formed into “A” Foreign Service Battalion MGC, from the cadre of the 8th Battalion MGC, from France. Training commenced. Designation of the unit changed to the 8th (special) Battalion MGC, under the command of Lt. Col. W A T B Somerville DSO (Royal Artillery) from 12th April 1919. The Battalion was stationed at Crowborough Camp, Sussex on the 15th April, and on the 7th May was warned for North Russia.

On the 12th May, the Battalion entrained for Newcastle upon Tyne, via London. The Battalion boarded HMT Zyarietza the next day, and was given a good send off, all ship yard work ceased temporarily and all steamers on the Tyne blew their hooters.

Arrived in Murmansk on 20th May and on the 24th May, sailed with convoy and icebreakers for Archangel. Arrived in Archangel- Smolny Barracks, on 26th May 1919. On the 27th May marched to Sobornaia Wharf. On the 9th June embarked on Ferryboat and proceeded up the Dwina (River).

Bunt was a keen sportsman in India (and fisherman at home). He brought home many trophies, including the then record GUR head which hangs (2007) in Reendesert. Many of his heads were donated to the Natural History museum in Dublin.
He improved the gardens at Reendesert with the assistance of Jamsie, the gardener.. There was a particularly fine water garden.

For many years, he was a director of Clinch & Co of Witney, but he would not have been described as a businessman. He, with Jim, was one of his mother’s executors. It was alledged that their inexperience of the business world lead to the substantial dilution of family control of the Brewery by the sale of shares to Mr Lowe, the Manager. The administration of his mother’s estate lead to enormous dissension among the family, particularly between Bunt and Tetty; but members of the family kept taking ‘sides’ for many years, even after Bunt’s death.

Regi always referred to him as being conscious of his position as eldest son. He evidently did not like being seen carrying parcels. He was quiet and somewhat retiring. He was inclined to procrastinate; as a result, he didn’t ‘put his affairs in order’ after his mother’s death in 1949. He was a heavy smoker and ultimately succumbed to lung cancer.
WBRBS from personal knowledge and conversation with Regi

All we know from the Somerville Index is that

first husband was Alan Ferguson. Further researches reveal that his middle name was Campbell, that he was the son of Surgeon-Major William Ferguson and that by the time he married in 1908 his father was dead. During the Great War he served

France, arriving there on 1 Oct 1915. The archives from The Times mention his interests in New South Wales, Australia. The probate records show that his estate was worth £33,475 3s 9d when he died, which is worth over £1,040,000 today.

We also know that he converted Reendesert Lodge from two cottages. It was situated on about 60 acres beside the sea in Bantry Bay; there was a small harbour. Alan Ferguson kept an ocean going yacht. His Australian interests prospered substantially and were enjoyed by Kitty long after his death. Regi maintained that he married Kitty in middle age, after she and Bunt had met, under pressure from her father. The inference was that he supported his father in law financially.

After Kitty’s death, Reendesert, and contents (including Somerville property), passed to Roberta Power, the daughter of Kit Power, daughter of Marjorie Barclay, Kitty’s sister. Roberta sold off much of the land, attempted to run the house as a guest house, but then married a Canadian, surnamed Lank, and moved to Canada. The property now belongs to friends of WBRBS and Manon. Bunt’s record GUR head still hangs in the hall.
Kitty had quite a personality, a foil to Bunt’s retiring nature. She was smart, both in appearance and wit.

Transcript of Letter from Jim Somerville to his neice, Merlie Truell.

It was very nice to get your letter, or rather half letter, today. The only reason I did not write to you before was that I really had nothing to say. I could have said “I’m quite well, thank you” and “How are you”, but that would not have filled up a letter. It would not have interested you very much to know that I had had a very good breakfast today, thank you very much, and had also had a very nice lunch, and was looking forward to my tea and dinner later on – and as nothing very much goes on between there would not have been very much more to say. I could of course also say that the sun was shining, the rain was raining, the wind was winding, but as these are their usual occupations the news would hardly have been wildly exciting.

Now I can only tell you of my occupation for the last few days. On Sunday I went over to see some people in Surrey, and spent the afternoon eating plums and playing with two little girls aged 3½ and 1½ or thereabouts. On Monday afternoon I went to a place about 30 miles away and fished. I caught 4 small fish which I threw back and also hooked two large fish which went back of their own accord before they were landed. I had dinner there, played bridge after dinner and got back here at 1.30 in the morning. Yesterday afternoon I went to see Heather and Uncle Pat. I found Uncle Pat in bed with malaria. I came back here in pouring rain, and went to the cinema in the evening. Today I am busy writing this.

I am very glad to hear Julie had a bath last week, even although she did not expect it at the moment. I hope she got no ill after effects from it, as your Aunt Cecil seems to have got from a similar rash act. I hope she has by now fully recovered.

Do write me some more long letters and don’t mind very much if I don’t answer them at once. You see, I don’t have very much to write about, and I can’t always hope to make them as interesting and newsy as this one. You’ve got much more to write about.
Give my love to every one

Dorothy Rooke, who was a bridesmaid at Jim (0663) and Greta’s wedding, used to contrast the Starkey family and guests with the Somerville family; she said the former were rather grand and stuffy, while the latter were having a good time. She was mortified that the Somerville children were to be seen and not heard, being confined to the Nursery floor. Somewhere WBRBS has a family picture taken after the wedding on the steps of the garden front of Norwood. Many years later (59 to be precise), after Greta’s funeral, which Tommy Rooke, Peter Truell and WBRBS attended, a similar Starkey/Somerville photograph was taken on the same steps.

Greta very kindly gave WBRBS Jim’s second signature ring for his son James, following a visit to Dargle Hill. His first signature ring (given to Jim by his mother) was lost while bathing in a lake in Kashmir. During the visit, it was discovered that the Starkey family were neighbours and friends of Sir Charles Birkin, who had lived at Dargle Hill from about 1950 to 1961 and been responsible for enlarging and considerably improving the property.

Greta, who had a wide circle of friends, even while she and Jim lived at Clermont for a while in 1949/1950, always appeared ‘vague’ and some would say ‘scatty’. When she moved to Queensgate Mews, she led a secluded life. Jim had contemplated living in Ireland when they were at Clermont, but his early death intervened.

Cr 1st Baronet Starkey of Norwood Park in the King’s Birthday and Jubilee Honours 1935

For some 800 years, Norwood Park was owned by the Archbishop of York as part of the Manor of Southwell which was given to him in 956 by the Saxon King. In early medieval times a Deer Park was created in a tract of woodland pasture, notable for its fine specimen oak trees and fish ponds, by enclosing it within an earthwork that still exists.

Edward Cludd, the estate manager at the time of the Civil War used his friendship with Oliver Cromwell to acquire the Park. He built the first ‘pretty little brick house’. Too small for John Sutton who later took over the lease of the Park, it was replaced by the present handsome Georgian mansion in the 1760’s. At the same time, the Park was landscaped with the addition of the Temple, two more fishponds and the Lime Avenue.

Since 1881, when Lewis Starkey moved his family from Yorkshire, Norwood has been home to five generations. John Ralph Starkey planted the first Bramley orchard in 1910 when MP for Newark. His son William and grandson John have kept the fruit growing tradition alive which also includes a substantial strawberry enterprise.

The plan was to get into a sack with room for plenty of stuffing all round it and to be carried out of the camp as “waste paper.”

Everything was ready and I was actually sitting in the sack as a final test when the alarm went, a Russian had been caught trying to get away, a roll call was held, and all the camp searched. Everything to do with my scheme was founds, framework, maps and all, this was followed by arrest and court martial. The sentence was only a fortnight’s solitary confinement, but it cooled one’s ardour for the time being.

The Russian attempt had been a good show. An aged general, over sixty years of age, crawled down a drain and was only waiting for darkness to emerge outside the camp when he was discovered by the cleaner of the said drain.

Our excitement as regards the course of the war at this time was very intense, especially as the Germans continually claimed victories, the Somme battles were ranging and periodically Zeppelins passed
over the camp on their way to carry out their bombing raids on England.
There followed the cold winter of 1916-1917 and two of us decided to make use of this cold spell to bring off an escape.

To get out of the camp by the main exit one had to pass through three gates, the innermost one of which was always kept locked; the outer two, though some high iron railings and the outer barbed wire fencing, were not locked, but had a sentry patrolling in between them. The outer windows of the building we lived in looked out on to these iron railings. These windows
ere securely fastened up by iron hasps, but we noticed that if we coul
only get out of one of these window
we would avoid having to negotiate the locked door, and by scaling the railings when the sentry was not looking, we would only have one more gate to get through to be free. We made our plan.

Everything went well. For months we worked on the making of German uniforms in which we dressed and made ourselves into quite respectable-looking German soldiers. One very snowy night, after hours of patient work – as it had to be noiseless – we sawed the iron fasteners of the outer window. The sentry was sheltering from the snow behind a pillar in the railings on the far side of the gate from us. Once out of the window, we quickly scaled the railings, expecting
a bullet in the back of our anatomies. We turned right and walked straight out of the outer gate. All was clear, but just at

hat moment a German under-officer was coming down the road. He accosted us. Where were we German soldiers going at that time of the night, what were our names, would we be back soon. One of us could speak German, the other hardly. Hesitation caused suspicion. We were brought back to the guard-room. In the bright light our disguise was easily discernible. Cells till morning for further investigation.
Further investigation led to a remand.

Additional Research about Strohen POW camp:

2ND Lt Robert Stanley Capon was held at Strohen for about 4 months before being transferred to Holzminden in the late autumn of 1917. It is likely that he was there when Pat Somerville made his home run.

The camp was situated on a moor north of the road between the villages of Ströhen and Wagenfeld. The camp accommodation was in wooden huts and had previously housed Russian and Serbian p.o.w.’s. At Ströhen the food was very poor and many of the prisoners were badly undernourished. The camp had its own group of thespians; one review they put on began with the words “Come to sunny Ströhen with its golden sands and its beautiful blue lagoons”. Capon describes the camp as a detestable spot. The golden sands were a mess of dirty earth; the “blue lagoons” were two of three muddy ponds intended to drain off the all too plentiful water from the peat bog in which the camp was situated. The camp huts were not very clean and the mattresses were stuffed with paper. At the end of the first six weeks one of the lumps was a ginger beer bottle! Despite all this he notes it was the pleasantest camp he visited, across the moorland was the Ems river and once across that it was only a few miles to the Dutch border. He notes “The whole camp was escape mad” every two or three weeks they were heartened with the news of another successful escapee reaching England. Capon joined a group of men who were tunnelling. The tunnel ran from a point beneath the floor of a hut situated about 20 ft from the boundary of the camp. As there was no cover outside the camp at the point selected under whose shelter they could emerge, they decided on the following scheme. When they were sure they had arrived at a point a yard or two outside the barbed wire boundary fence they would work towards the surface, supporting the earth with props until only a few inches of earth remained. They intended to allow this to fall in by removing the props at the moment when the sentry was at the end of his beat furthest removed from the tunnel and bolt for it. A dark night was to be chosen and the party would consist of six men. The first job was to calculate the distance required, and then they removed several floor boards which were fitted with dummy nails. Tunnelling began through the soft earth, very soft, after a few feet of tunnelling the roof fell in, fortunately before they emerged from under the hut. After observing that the boards used to support tier beds were hard and not very springy they and it was decided to use them in an inverted V structure, the beds were duly partially stripped of boards as needed with the unfortunate next donor being distracted by a visit to the canteen whist the boards were removed. The next problem to overcome was the foul air and the need to provide fresh air to the worker at the face. This was overcome buy the construction of a centrifugal pump using a cigarbox and pasteboard but they were delayed by the construction of a pipe for sometime. This was resolved by wrapping cloth on a broom handle, then coating with adhesive purchased in the canteen and then removing the handle. Work continued under the constant fear of being found out. Capon never got to see the tunnel finished. He attempted to escape from the camp bathroom. This had been used by a chap called Knight to make the first successful escape. Capon and an accomplice devised a plan to remain in the room following a bathing parade. There was a barred window at the side of the bathroom facing away from the camp and a short distance away a boiler on wheels with an opening at one end provided with a swinging door. The boiler did not appear to be used and he thought how pleasant it would be to be ensconced in it waiting for nightfall. The one problem was the bars on the window which were of iron about 1 inch wide and 1 ½ inches thick. Mentioning this to a friend he was informed that a table knife could be used to cut metal that was not too hard by striking the edges of two knives together so as to make a saw. They immediately brought some knives from the canteen, prepared them and tried them on a metal bar of a window in their hut. To their surprise they found that rapid progress could be made; the knife became ineffective after a few minutes but with a supply of newly prepared knives they calculated that if the material of the bars of the bath room window was not harder than that which they used in their experiment they could cut through a bar in about twenty minutes. The friend went with the first bathing party and cut through the bar as far as he could. Capon was to follow in the next parade and finish the job and hide in the boiler. A distraction was arranged to fool the guard counting the party that all was correct. The plan went as expected, the bar was cut, Capon was having smuggled in a haversack with food, compass and a map, removed the severed bar and stepped through the window – and as he did a German solider with a rifle stepped out of the door adjoining the window. Capon was sentenced to a month solitary confinement in the camp, which he describes at “the pleasantest period I spent as a prisoner of war”. The routine was not too harsh and by bribing the guards small comforts could be obtained. Exercise was taken in pairs on the quadrangle, and improvised game of squash and tennis could be played against a wall. Chess was played by shouting the moves to your opponent although confusion could arise if several games were in progress at the same time. There was no close supervision in the evenings and the men took full advantage visiting each others rooms and arranged gramophone and bridge parties. During his four month stay at Ströhen some 20 odd men are thought to have escaped.

WBRBS remembers Pat as being a thoroughly outgoing person, making the most of every situation. A vivid memory is the enthusiasm with which he used to enter into the game of ‘Murder’ at Clermont in 1945/6. As the victim, he got hold of somebody’s lipstick and ‘slashed’ his throat, groaning in agony.

Story also has it that all the girls fell for him, although he hadn’t the looks of his brothers. His charm attracted, among others, Diana Somerville, one of the Cork family, and most recently, the late Hilda Sandys (of Dargle Hill) told us how she used to cycle the 15 miles to Clermont for the dancing in the hope that Pat would be at home. RMJBS related how Heather(0668) was invited to Clermont by Jim(0663), but ended up with Pat!

Transcripts of Letters to Merlie Truell:

It was very good to get your combined letter the other day which I found easier & more delightful to read than you will this (possibly and probably – but not certainly – ha – that was a joke!). I would have sent a note in reply earlier but for that beastly malaria bug which walked out again and left me (illegible) for some days.

I’m having a very good time here with “Nauntie” and all the family – but as your great brains may well imagine, rather a “buzzy” one, both from taking quinine and the general rush of “trousseau” and that that sort of thing. Four of us are going to the theatre in London on Saturday & I may be crossing over to Ireland that night – or if not on Sunday or Monday as I want to have some time at Clermont before you all go. I’ve such a lot of letters to write, I must really end having only scribbled a very few lines I know – but you understand, couldn’t he?!
PS to Julie – many thanks for your 2nd letter. Very many thanks for the 3rd.

PPS to Merlie – very late I know, but all best wishes for your last birthday. I’m going to London tomorrow and will see what I can do there for it for Nauntie and myself as there are no shops here. P.

You have probably noticed that I left a good many days between getting your letter + picking up my pen to write in reply – The truth is really that, firstly, I’m always bad at raising energy to write, and secondly, that there was nothing interesting to write about before - there isn’t now, but never mind –

It has been terribly quiet since you all left, and we have really done nothing interesting since. I’ve had a couple of exciting golf matches against Ede + Bill Herafath, but, of course, as we had no respectable caddies they fell rather flat!! We’ve now won three matched to their two – but more by flukes than good play.

I liked your description of the journey over – the crossing is always bad enough, but when you’ve several young relatives being continuously ill at intervals (or even feeling like it) it must be rather worse.

I have now started to work up for my exam for promotion (it is now May 16th) + so I am all alone in the house as the others have all gone to Glendalough – One of my exams comes off in July + the other in October – but I can always work much better when I know there’s no one else anywhere near – so I hope they will go out very often –
I hear Mike is better – good – but that poor Rachael [feeling] miserable. Give her my love + tell her that Count Whatnot hopes she will soon be better.
I must now get on with work again – good luck during the term,

Following a long illness from Blackwater Fever in 1934, from which he maintained he only recovered through the ministration of a drunken Irish doctor, he, Maudie and Juanita, accompanied by the redoubtable nanny, Miss Clague, sailed for recuperation and leave in Europe in March 1935. Maudie, who had a sore throat on boarding the
Madura in Mombasa, immediately developed what was believed to be meningitis and died suddenly two days out and was buried at sea ( see entry at (0671)
. Regi, under pressure from his mother, didn’t return to Kenya for many years, but retained the farm until 1945.

Following his marriage to Honor (0673), Regi built Ruwenzori on an elevated site with a panoramic view to remind him of the open spaces of Kenya and started market gardening until war broke out in 1939 when he volunteered and joined the Royal Welch Fusiliers.
Served World War 11: Lt Royal Welch Fusiliers 1939 – 1941
War Work with Sentinel Wagon Works

By 1941, although only 44, he was deemed ‘too old’ for the Army, so was demobbed (?) and spent the remainder of the war making Bren Gun carriers at Sentinel. He and the family lived throughout the war at Onslow Hall (see entry at (0673)) where Honor was matron at St Georges School. Regi was stationed when in the RWF in several places nearby.

After the war, Regi and the family returned to Ireland, lived initially at Clermont while Ruwenzori was tenanted, and started the market garden again. He continued with this, and running the property at Clermont for his mother and, after her death in 1949, for his brother Bunt. In 1953, he retired to Dublin.

Following Bunt’s death in 1951, Regi, with Cecil (0675) and Tetty (0680), spent much time closing gaps in the Somerville family genealogical information which had been assembled in the Somerville Records which had been given to him. He was encouraged by his sisters, especially Tetty, to establish his claim to the Somerville of Dublin Baronetcy which had been dormant since the death of his cousin, the 2nd Lord Athlumney (0638), in 1929. He and Tetty worked on this with the help of Walter Verco, Chester Herald, Sir Austin Strutt, Registrar of the Baronetage, and Sir Arthur Bellew, then Garter King of Arms. Substantial progress was made between 1955 and 1966, but Regi eventually lost heart and got ill.

As a boy, Regi played in the endless hockey games that the Clermont regime allowed. He adored his father and picked up a certain manual dexterity and interest in photography from him. In his youth, he was a keen fisherman and shot. When Bertie Truell lived at Clonmannon, he spent much of his young life shooting and wild fowling there. Always interested in‘growing things’, in later years, he kept a wonderful town garden in Ailesbury Road, full of colour and scent. His great love was his greenhouse and, particularly, the propagation and growth of cacti.

Regi was intensely reserved, as were, but to a lesser extent, his brothers, Bunt(0660) and Jim(0663): he found it difficult to communicate with outsiders and led a lonely life. The extraordinary way in which they were brought up may have been responsible. While Bunt and Jim did go to primary schools for short periods, the whole family were educated privately by Governesses and Tutors, the Misses Attwood, Shillaker, Tedder and Mr Burks among others. Regi lacked the gravitas of Bunt, the angular curiosity of Jim, and, although he had a quiet, but mischievous sense of humour, he hadn’t the outgoing spontaneity of Pat(0667). Like his father, he was particularly good at carpentry, and generally managed to put right all things that stopped working: eg bells, lights, taps, clocks etc While Pat overcame the disadvantages of their closeted childhood, having a period of peace time training before the traumas of WW1, Regi went straight from the schoolroom and the protected environment of Clermont to the Army at war and was in the trenches before he was twenty. When he did eventually find a life of his own in Kenya, he lost his wife within a few years of marriage. At home, except when useful, he was sorely patronized by his siblings; he became known as, and was referred to as, ‘poor Regi’. Honor suffered similarly; far from being congratulated on the birth of her son, she used to record the incident when she was shut up in the linen room at Clermont by one of Regi’s sisters and sisters in law as they were all jealous that she, Regi’s second wife, had produced the only ‘Somerville’ boy. But, like Regi, Honor was practical and helpful when called upon, and, unlike Regi, she was a manager. Manon (0683) feels Regi suffered throughout his adult life from a silent depression

brought on by the horrors of WW1, the disappointment of the Kenya farming venture after Blackwater Fever, the death of Maudie, the refusal of his mother to allow a return to Kenya and the financial difficulties following his mother’s death
: Bill’s(0682) memory of his father is the way in which he constantly stood in front of a window staring into space as if wondering what might have been.

Letter from Margaret Hall Somerville to Merlie Truell written from Regi’s home (called Clermont) in Kenya.

I am only sending a short letter to tell you we are quite well. I am having a delightful time here – life here is so free and everything is so interesting – the days seem to fly by. We are always busy but seem to get very little accomplished – there is such a vast amount to be done. The natives are so slow & lazy and it is most difficult to get enough of them – they are too always wanting [illeg] [illeg] and their wages revised – people say that before long there will have to be a great deal more machinery used out here it is so difficult to get labourers + of course oxen are very slow but unfortunately they have to be used as horses will not live here.

It is about impossible to get more than one acre of land ploughed in the day + that takes 16 oxen – 3 boys to drive & guide and a master to lead – so you can tell the time it takes to do things & the noise they make shouting and roaring one would really think there was something exciting happening.

This morning Uncle Regi & I went to Kitale on business – it is a really nice little place which has grown so quickly too – a year ago there was very little [illeg] and a few huts – now they have some quite nice little houses with verandahs + such pretty gardens full of flowers, fruit and vegetables - the strawberries are in blossom. On our way back we called to see some friends of Uncle Regis – a Mr and Mrs Roberts – they are young + quite nice. They have two little girls aged 31/2 years & 7 weeks. They have the sweetest little house with a verandah covered with creepers - & a lovely view. I shall describe all these places to you when we meet.

There is lots of game around here – this morning just after breakfast a buck passed very near the house – constantly we see them. I hear there are lots of hyenas - & zebras – but I have not seen them anywhere. I am told too that an odd lion & leopard + elephant pass by. I hope they will stay away during my visit. There are most wonderful wild flowers + such a variety – they grow in such out of the way places. I never go in the long grass to look for them, I have never seen any reptiles but I am afraid of them & [illeg] too. The weather here changes so quickly, it may be very hot- when suddenly a strong wind may get up & heavy rain comes over – often thunder - & it gets quite chilly but as a rule it is hot from about 10 till 4 o/c – at 6 o/c one is very glad of a fire and the mornings are cold too. We have our breakfast at 7.30, cup of tea at 10.30 – lunch 12.30 – tea 4 o/c – dinner 7 o/c & I go to bed about 9 to 9.30 o/c. The day passes so quickly although always busy so little seems to be done – there is such a lot of work before us – it will take a long time to get the place in order. But it is most interesting - we both love the work and the place.

I am sure you are all busy preparing for Xmas and the holidays. I hope you will have a very nice time & good weather – not too cold – it is difficult here to believe we are near Xmas it is so warm. Please give my best love to all & keep lots to yourself- [illeg illeg] to mother,

Cecil, who had wanted to marry, in her younger days, a young man named ? Davis, an RIC constable, a

Cecil was a lifelong social historian and genealogist who spent most of her life building on the research into
the Somerville and related families which had occupied her father for upwards of fifty years in the second
half of the nineteenth and early years of the twentieth century. In particular, after her marriage to Henry
Rooke, she devoted her skills to exploring the history of that family and recording it for posterity. A glance
at the introduction to the Collection of the Rooke Family Papers, now housed in the National Library of
Ireland will show the depth and breadth of her interest.

The Somerville Family at Clermont about 1908
Many of the notes in the Somerville Index were taken by Cecilia E M B Rooke between 1912 and 1914 at the Record Office Dublin.
For the Collection of the Rooke Family Papers

Cecil B. Rooke [as she always signed herself] was already a keen genealogist and it is the written records of her research into the ancestry of the Rooke family that form the main part of this collection. In the first year of her

marriage, she extracted Rooke wills and marriage licences in the Public Record Office, at the Four Courts, Dublin. These extracts were invaluable as they established the early generations of the Rooke family in Dublin and of course the originals were destroyed in 1922. Although she appears to have done considerable research on the genealogy of the Rooke family in the early years of her marriage and, no doubt, was able to establish a family tree [see Ms. 33,588 letter dated 19 Feb. 1916], it was not until the early 1950s that she set it out in a fully comprehensive manner. This was done to enable her eldest son, Colonel H.T.B.B.Rooke [Tommy Rooke], to apply to the Chief Herald of Ireland for a grant of arms [see Ms.33,597]

Despite rearing four children during the 1920s and 1930s, Cecil B. Rooke continued to take an active interest in family history, however it is evident from her papers that she had more time for research from the 1940s onwards. Her interests extended way beyond the Rooke family, as she traced back the antecedents of each female that married into the family. She relied heavily on printed works, such as the various volumns published by Sir Bernard Burke and on original sources such as parish registers, deeds and other manuscript material. She was driven by family members to churchyards all over the country where she took notes on gravestone memorials. The permanent notes [see Ms. 33,585] she compiled on so many family names are the culmination of all this research.

She was particularly interested in her own genealogy, that of the Somerville family and this is reflected in her papers. In the late 19th century her father B. A. Somerville gathered information about the family, including extracts from many Somerville wills in the Public Record Office [see Ms. 33,586 (1)] . Cecil B. Rooke

used his research (c) but she also accumulated a considerable amount of information herself about the Somervilles and their connections, such as the Bellingham, Quayle, O’Connor and many other families. It is apparent that the O’Connor family (d), with their Rolfe and Walplate connections, were one of the last families for whom she compiled permanent notes, as were the Chambalyne family, Irish connections of her

daughter in law Pia Dormer. The permanent notes for these families were ready for filing when the collection was deposited in the National Library. I suggest that George Truell’s notes from the 1960s on his mother should be incorporated here, BUT there are uncertainties, inaccuracies and errors so the following should be approached with caution:

1 While I am aware of the family’s house in Harcourt St, Dublin, as far as I can see, the family lived in rented houses in and around Wicklow from 1888 to 1895 when, having bought Clermont the previous year and renovated it, they moved in. The idea that BAS lived in these rented houses on his own, except when babies were being born, is unrealistic. BAS, in his office journal, is scrupulous in entering up the various duties and time taken on them, and his absences on leave. It is true that he visits Dublin fairly frequently on 12 hrs leave of absence, but I take it that this is not to visit wife and children, so much as parents,

brother and to follow up his endless genealogical research. As far as I can see, they were at Seaview in 1888, Friars Hill 1890 – 1892, Ballyhenry 1894 and again at Seaview in 1895 before going to Clermont. On looking at George’s notes on BAS, there seems to be doubt about the time the family lived in Dublin. There he suggests they went to Harcourt Street in 1887. They were in Queenstown until the end of 1887 and then in Seaview in 1888, while he says here that they went to Harcourt St in 1892 so Georges two accounts don’t reconcile. I am pretty sure the period in Harcourt Street was 1892 to 1894 when, having bought Clermont, they returned to Wicklow, to Ballyhenry. Further enquiry needed; I must have letters.

2 There is a ref to the sale of Ballyhenry to raise death duties by The Rev WHA Truell. This is not correct. The doctor, Henry Pomeroy Truell, who had Clonmannon before his cousin,The Rev WHAT, had married Elizabeth Rolleston-Spunner,, grand daughter of a John Richards, of the Court of Exchequer.She looked after her two Richards cousins, Charles William and Ida at Clonmannon. My father had been led to believe that there was a question over the legitimacy of one or both of them. He said that Charles William, known as Billy Richards, behaved oddly and certainly looked odd; his two eyes were each of a different colour. He used to come to Clermont and would leave his wife in the car while he came in and was entertained. He had married Kathleen Stamper from NewtownMtKennedy in 1904 whereupon, they moved into Ballyhenry which was, in due course, transferred by voluntary transfer to them. I knew Kathleen Richards, as a fairly elderly lady; she was still at Ballyhenry when I was growing up and lived there with her widowed daughter, Joyce Brown (whose husband was killed in the Spanish Civil War) and her daughter Bumble (otherwise Noreen but later calling herself Loretta). There were childrens’ parties. In due course, Bumble was at TCD with me. There lies another story; she was sadly killed in a car accident shortly after making a ‘joke’ will in the TCD library, in which she left her estate, including Ballyhenry which her grandmother had transferred to her, all on various ‘amusing’ conditions; the tabloids had a field day.
3 The field backing on to the side lane (the Bullock Walk) at Clermont, and between it and the straight garden path, was called KEOGH’s Field.

4 The reference to Mr Tombe was to Bergie Tombe. He was the Tighes’ Agent at Rossana and, along with Dr Lyndon, was one of the few people regularly entertained at Clermont. He lived at Rossana Cottage, where Manon and I lived when we were first married, now, somewhat pretentiously called ‘The Dower House’ which it never was.
5 Jim was the first person in the family to have a car, I think, a de Dion Bouton ?, not sure of the second word.

6 The pitchfork incident is unknown to me; Pat was 17 and Regi was 14 rather too mature ? to be fooling with pitchforks, and if his boot and foot were really pierced, not to be forgotten by Regi. The two were very close throughout their lives.
7 Uncle Tom Rolfe was the Rector or Vicar of Kirk Bramwith in Yorkshire, The Rev PB Johnson was Rector of Wicklow.
8 The ‘CLADDAGH’ was a waterside settlement in Galway said to be as old as the Armada. It is part of Irish history that many Spaniards were washed up in Galway B

ay; in fact most of them were washed up further north around the Donegal coast. They are often said to be responsible for the dark haired Celtic stock. The description of the ring is accurate, but I wasn’t aware it served as a wedding ring, though this seems reasonable.
9 Keenagh Hill is, I think, the property more recently called the Khyber Pass; it is situated at the top of a cliff above the railway line.
10 I don’t know of a Maine House in or near Wicklow; I wonder is somebody misreading Marlton House.
11 Ballyvolan is near Newcastle, not near Ashford.
I hesitate to write about your grandmother, especially as I have few detailed memories of her.

What I do recall is that she was a ‘difficult person’, both in her own family and in the wider family. She always seemed to be at odds with one or more of her children; particularly Toby and Ray. I had experience of her refusal to talk to members of her family at Tetty’s funeral which I had to arrange. She would not go in the same car as Ray from the Church to Putney vale, so there was a row as to who would go in which car – I don’t now remember the detail, but she really was impossible at the time. Her infrequent visits to Ireland were approached with concern, if not dread, by the family here, so much so that we discouraged her from attending my father’s funeral for fear of a scene. On the other hand, when she came to Cecil’s funeral, I think that was the time, she came here to see us accompanied by Mary, George’s wife; she was sweetness itself on that occasion.
